# [Battle Scar – Remembering the Poet Behind the Power. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #MaxWebster #PyeDubois #Rush #NeilPeart#KimMitchell](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/03/battle-scar-remembering-the-poet-behind-the-power-musicislife-tedtockscovers-maxwebster-pyedubois-rush-neilpeart-kimmitchell/)

[October 3, 2026 October 3, 2026](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/03/battle-scar-remembering-the-poet-behind-the-power-musicislife-tedtockscovers-maxwebster-pyedubois-rush-neilpeart-kimmitchell/) ~ [tedlindsay0170](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/author/tedlindsay0170/) ~ [Leave a comment](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/03/battle-scar-remembering-the-poet-behind-the-power-musicislife-tedtockscovers-maxwebster-pyedubois-rush-neilpeart-kimmitchell/#respond)

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PMM6Bhwpy0M)

Some songwriters never stand behind a microphone, yet their words echo as loud as the people singing them.

I am thinking of writers like Robert Hunter, Bernie Taupin, Shel Silverstein, Peter Sinfield and Norman Whitfield. I could go on. It’s a fascinating subject because they are stars in every right, but rarely did they accept the spotlight.

Pye Dubois is one of those writers. Most casual fans know Dubois from ‘Tom Sawyer’, clearly his most recognizable song.

> [Tom Sawyer – A monumental track from Moving Pictures by Rush and a few personal reflections. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #Rush #NeilPeart #PyeDubois #Alex Lifeson #GeddyLee #AlexisonFire #TenaciousD #StringCheeseIncident #JackBlack#ImagineDragons](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2019/09/12/tom-sawyer-a-monumental-track-from-moving-pictures-by-rush-and-a-few-personal-reflections-musicislife-tedtockscovers-rush-neilpeart-pyedubois-alex-lifeson-geddylee-alexisonfire-tenaciousd/)

But if you want to understand what made Dubois special, you must dig a little deeper, and Battle Scar’ is a perfect place to start.

Here is where I should add some context. Pye Dubois was a Canadian poet and lyricist who wrote for every Max Webster album. Over roughly two decades he also collaborated with Neil Peart on four Rush songs. In addition to his contribution to ‘Tom Sawyer’ he co-wrote ‘Force 10’ from ‘Hold Your Fire’.

> We can rise and fall like empires  
> Flow in and out like the tide  
> Be vain and smart, humble and dumb  
> We can hit-and-miss like pride  
> Just like pride  
> We can circle around like hurricanes  
> Dance and dream like lovers  
> Attack the day like birds of prey  
> Or scavengers under cover, under cover”

Imagine; this was written almost forty years ago.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NS1lbRU0Fzw)

Then there was ‘Between Sun and Moon’ from ‘Counterparts’.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zsfgewRxwu8)

More on that album in a bit.

Then there was ‘Test for Echo’ the title track from Rush’s sixteenth studio album.

> Some kind of pictures on the sense o’clock news  
> Miles of yellow tape, silhouetted chalk lines  
> Tough-talking hood boys in pro-team logo knock-offs  
> Conform to uniforms of some corporate entity  
> Don’t change that station  
> It’s a Gangsta Nation  
> Now crime’s in syndication on TV”

One decade later, and Pye Dubois and Neil Peart effortless capture the present and predict the future all at once.

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=deUirMqTV6A)

His partner in Max Webster; the band’s front man Kim Mitchell, described his contribution in this way.

> You sure knew how to jam with the English language and bring it!

Dubois didn’t hand you a neat narrative. He handed you a canvas and trusted you to feel what was on it. In 2021, Dubois and Mitchell were inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame, which says plenty about how far his influence reached.

‘Battle Scar’ might be the finest example of this talent at full strength. It is a gripping, dramatic piece, and it sounds even bigger because Rush lent their epic talent to the recording. Geddy Lee’s unmistakable voice and the band’s precision give the track a weight that matches its subject matter. But the music is only half the story. The real power is in the lyrics.

What makes ‘Battle Scar’ so alluring is how it treats human conflict. Dubois doesn’t write a flag-waving anthem or a simple ‘war is bad’ slogan. Instead, he looks across a millennium of human history and suggests that over time, the violence has left marks that never fully heal. Figuratively, that scar becomes the central image of the song. A wound closes, but the mark remains as proof of what happened. Applied to humanity, that idea is chilling. Every generation inherits the scars of the ones before it, and sadly, we keep adding new ones.

This is why the song works as a veiled protest. It is way more than a hard rock anthem. Protest music is often direct and loud, but Dubois builds his statement through imagery and atmosphere. The lyrics move through scenes of conflict, conquest, and suffering without pinning themselves to a single war or era. That approach is brilliant. Because the song isn’t tied to one event, it can speak to many. Within the economy of words, we are taken to ancient battlefields, modern conflicts, and every atrocity in between. A listener in 1980, and a listener today can both find their own world inside it. The song accuses humanity of a crime. Allowing history to repeat itself, and it does so without ever lecturing.

If you are a fan of Max Webster and Rush, tell me…Did you know ‘Battle Scar’ was a history lesson baked into a power rock jam?

Within this context there is a sense of grief running underneath. The song doesn’t celebrate victors. It lingers on the cost, on the people who carry the damage long after the fighting stops. That emotional honesty is part of why the track hits so hard, even for listeners who can’t quite explain what the words mean. Like Neil Peart’s masterpiece ‘Bravado’ from ‘Roll the Bones’ you feel the weight before you decode the poetry.

> And if the music stops, there’s only the sound of the rain  
> All the hope and glory, all the sacrifice in vain”

We WILL pay the price.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUSpBAmSMb8)

These are the themes that run through the lyrical journey that Pye Dubois delivered. His wider career elaborates on this instinct. His poem ‘There Is a Lake Between Sun and Moon’ inspired Rush to write many of the lyrics for the album ‘Counterparts’.

> There is a lake between sun and moon  
> Not too many know about  
> Some go there for their high noon  
> Some go there for their midnight moon  
> It is a moment between silence and shout  
> Maybe you, might as well me  
> Why the sun, why the sun  
> Say yes, say yes, ahh say yes to self-esteem  
> We want to escape because we don’t want to fall in  
> The signs are clear and so is the fear  
> We do not trust the firmness of the ground  
> Then say yes, say yes, ahh say yes to self-esteem  
> There is a fine place between actor and audience  
> This is the fine line  
> The fine line of living  
> This moment experienced  
> This fine deliverance  
> Do what you want to do in no ordinary way  
> Say what you need to say in no ordinary way  
> And sing what must be sung in no ordinary way  
> Say yes, ahh please, please say yes to self-esteem  
> Some go there for their high noon  
> Some go there for their midnight moon  
> It is the moment between silent and shout  
> This is a fine place  
> Faces face to face  
> These bonfire eyes  
> In the lake of the sky  
> It is our light to land and leave  
> Never so dark to unravel the weave  
> Never give up and never say die  
> Do what you need to do in no ordinary way  
> Say what you need to say in no ordinary way  
> And sing what must be sung in no ordinary way”

A poem inspiring a whole album tells you how rich and flexible his imagery was. Many writers supplied stories; Dubois offered the spark that lit the fire.

Looking back, his significance is clear. He proved that rock lyrics in their brevity could be literature, never losing their punch. He showed that a song can protest the worst parts of human history while still being thrilling to listen to. And in ‘Battle Scar’, he left us a reminder that the past never really leaves us, because we not only wear it, but we perpetuate the atrocities through crimes of commission and omission.

That is the mark of a great songwriter. Pye Dubois wrote words that make you think, make you feel, and perhaps most importantly, they make you want to hit replay.

As long as the music is playing, maybe the moral will penetrate our collective mind by osmosis?

Back to its origin, ‘Battle Scar’ was recorded live in studio in July of 1980, and released as the closing track on side one of ‘Universal Juveniles’ on this day 46 years ago.

The scorching album track was recorded at Phase One Studios in Toronto. Present at the session were members of Max Webster including Terry Watkinson on keyboards, and of course Geddy, Alex and Neil from Rush. The friendship between Rush and Max Webster went way back. Here is Kim Mitchell discussing the friendship that began just over 50 years ago when the members of Max Webster arrived in Toronto, making their way from their Sarnia roots.

> Rush were great friends and they always treated us as equals. There were so many beautiful moments, and they made touring so enjoyable. I can still picture Neil with a book and a pack of cigarettes. He was an intense dude, but so sweet once you knew him. I remember one day Alex couldn’t make sound-check, and I played with Ged and Neil.”

Max Webster’s debut album was released in May of 1976 on Rush manager Ray Danniels’s Taurus label. It was co-produced by long time Rush producer, Terry Brown. The close connection led to many live shows featuring Rush as the headliner and Max Webster as the supporting act.

Although the friendship was genuine, added importance could be found in Rush’s role as mentors as to how to survive in the music industry. Again, here is Kim Mitchell.

> Rush taught us that you should make your own decisions and not listen to record company bullshit. They were like, ‘This is our music, and these are our lives.”

By 1979 Max Webster had hit their commercial peak but at the same time they became victims of the harshness of the music industry. Following the success of ‘A Million Vacations’ the band’s U.S. label, refused to fund a European tour which would have seen the band headline. By the middle of 1980, Max Webster was determined to show Capitol they had made a mistake. They brought former Guess Who producer, Jack Richardson on board to work on the material that would become ‘Universal Juveniles’.

Among the collection of great songs was a demo for ‘Battle Scar.

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TP2sQEeVMuk)

All of this led to the two bands coming together on that summer day 46 years ago to create this relentless musical attack where every player fed off each other to create multiple layers of musical greatness. If you ever need a song to motivate you, this is it…

> Been in jail for a thousand years  
> Found a fist in an empty field  
> Only quarters for meals  
> Feel the way I feel  
>   
> Bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel  
>   
> Tried to understand the white man’s fears  
> Make ’em bend but they wouldn’t yield  
> Uncle Sam’s time is only a greased wheel  
> Feel the way I feel  
>   
> Bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel  
> I said bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel”

It borders on tragic that this would become Max Webster’s final studio album, but without the support from their label things slowly disintegrated. Kim Mitchell opted to leave the band in April of 1981 following a gig in Nashville. Was it fitting or sad that on this day Max Webster was the opening act for Rush?

For a quality take on the circumstances that led to ‘Battle Scar’ and the ‘Universal Juveniles’ album check out this excellent article from ‘Norseland’s Rock’.

> [THE STORY BEHIND THE SONG: «Battle Scar» by Max Webster and Rush](https://norselandsrock.com/battle-scar-max-webster-rush/)

Now, let’s look back at ‘Battle Scar’ through the years. Kim Mitchell had a successful solo career and much of his success can be attributed to his charisma and an always upbeat live show. That show always included ‘Battle Scar’ as an electrifying set closer. Here is Kim Mitchell out on the road in 1990.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YcnHH74p95w)

This is a real treat. Let’s go back to the 14 th Annual Andy Kim Christmas Show in December of 2018. Watch and listen as Alex joins Kim Mitchell and his band, but before we do, here is Alex speaking on the friendship between Rush and Max Webster and his memories of Pye Dubois.

> Those guys were big friends of ours. But Pye was a little mysterious – kind of a strange fellow! He was very quirky, a bit of a nut, but he did write great lyrics.”

Personal connections brought together through music are rarely forgotten.

[Video 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Fa8Co3BuJ4)

My search for pure cover versions led me to this interesting cover by Tom Gordon. This is well done. It stays true to the original with just enough of the artist’s obvious talent shining through.

[Video 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0nMPArI9rpA)

Most recently we find ourselves in 2023 at the Canada’s Walk of Fame Induction Ceremony with Gordie Johnson and Charlie Edward paying tribute to Max Webster. This recognition is well deserved.

[Video 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cA9_t8fDIHE)

If the verses of ‘Battle Scar’ mourn the wounds of history, the outro is where the song stops grieving and starts demanding change, or at least some semblance of action. The closing chant is relentless. It repeats like a rally cry, and each line turns the spotlight on a different kind of power. Those who destroy are told their time is coming. Those who profit from other people’s hunger are called out. Even the healers, the people trusted to care, are challenged to feel the pain they treat from a distance.

‘Battle Scar’ is Pye Dubois at his sharpest. He doesn’t name a villain, so the target keeps shifting with the times. Today, it’s easy to hear the chant aimed at war profiteers, corporations that thrive on scarcity, and institutions that talk about caring while staying insulated from consequences. The repetition makes it feel less like a lyric and more like an angry mob. A protest building volume until it can’t be ignored.

But where are all the people?

More than forty years later, the outro still works as a warning. It reminds the powers that be that people remember who caused the scars, and who profited from them. Great protest songs outlive their moment, and Pye Dubois understood that. “Battle Scar” doesn’t fade out quietly. It begs us to act.

> Bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel  
> I said bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel”

Upon Pye Dubois’ passing in September, Kim Mitchell shared his sadness with these words.

> Some say freedom is after the storm.”

True valour exists in rising to meet the challenge and inspiring people to join the fight.

Freedom is not a birthright. It has to be earned.

Warning:

This could get emotional.

I will begin by thanking my family and guiding light for banding together behind the scenes and getting me tickets to see Rush in Toronto on Tuesday August 11 th.

My oldest son Sebastian was the lucky recipient of the second ticket. Sebastian has spent a lot of 32 plus years absorbing Rush by osmosis and he openly states that his absolute indoctrination was watching Neil Peart play the drums at the Toronto SARS festival. In the present day, Sebastian performs admirably as a drummer for at least four bands in the Peterborough area.

As the concert day approached, we made plans to converge upon the city from opposite directions. I headed over from my home in Burlington. Heather sent me off, encouraging me to blast Rush from my car as I peeled out of the court. With ‘Tom Sawyer’ blaring, I was on my way.

I knew I would be hearing it again that evening. The question was where in the set it would appear. I’ll come back to that.

We met by Union Station at the corner of Bay and Front. From there we made our way across to SkyDome. Sebastian had let me know that the Toronto Blue Jays had recently unveiled a Joe Carter statue that commemorated his game winning 1993 World Series home run. The statue also lists the outstanding team that shared in the second of back-to-back World Series victories. It took me back. Pretty special.

Next up. Time to eat and the best part is we had time to kill. Relax. Chill. We had decided on a Mexican place over on The Esplanade called 3 Mariachis. Just taking it easy for a change was a nice feeling and spending time with Sebastian added to the moment. Above and beyond, the underlying anticipation of what the evening would bring added to the experience.

As the clockwork angels moved the hour hand toward 7:30 pm we headed past St. Lawrence Market and back up to Front Street and across to the venue. During the short walk I took the time to fire a message off to my cousin Christopher. He and his son Rowan were also in town for the show. I hit send and hoped that this would not be one of those times that the recipient did not see the message until the next day. Within seconds Christopher got back to me. They were making their way down from the Massey Hall area. We made plans to connect once we were both at the venue and despite the growing throng at Gate 3 we made this happen before they opened the doors. We were able to spend about 20 minutes together before the show started.

You know that line from ’Time Stand Still’?

> Summer’s going fast  
> Nights growing colder  
> Children growing up  
> Old friends growing older”

Through a combination of circumstance, busy schedules and distance Christopher and I have not seen each other in several years. Elements of the family connection have flowed through the annals of Ted Tocks Covers on several occasions. Back in 1982 when I saw Rush for the first time, our group included my cousin Shannon; Christopher’s sister. I also haven’t seen her in too long.

Time stand still…Please…Freeze…

Anyway, despite a six-year age difference Christopher and I have a very similar taste in music and through the years some of the nicest comments about Ted Tocks features have come from Christopher’s direction. Like me, he is a natural empath who feels music. His ability to cope with the enormous challenges life throws one’s way through song has served him well. One of the positive aspects of social media is the ability to stay connected through messages and passing commentary, but nothing beats real human connection.

As showtime approached we went to our respective seats, but not before arranging to meet during the intermission.

From our vantage point Sebastian and I had a birds-eye view of the entire venue. We drank in the atmosphere as the minute hand hit the bottom of the clock. The anticipation was palpable. We took our cue from the side stage concert attendees who noted the arrival of Loren Gold and Anika Nilles and as the lights dimmed the arena roared as one. > [School/Bloody Well Right – Somewhere Along the Way We Forgot the Golden Rule. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #Supertramp #RickDavies#RogerHodgson](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/06/school-bloody-well-right-somewhere-along-the-way-we-forgot-the-golden-rule-musicislife-tedtockscovers-supertramp-rickdavies-rogerhodgson/)

When I set down to write this feature, I was aiming to share how some songs make you stop everything and listen. ‘School’ and ‘Bloody Well Right’ still do that to me.

Is it the harmonica? The longing vocals? The piano that wanders off on its own mid-song? Or is it that so few writers today hold the establishment to account, and we need them more than ever?

In early September I marked the first anniversary of Rick Davies’ passing through these timeless Supertramp tracks. Davies’ bluesy piano is the backbone of these two tracks, but the feature reminds us that this was a partnership. Roger Hodgson brought the melody and the bruised sensitivity; Davies brought the grit.

Yin and yang.

‘School’ grew from Hodgson’s boarding school years at Stowe, a sensitive boy sent away to be made sensible. Schools, he says, teach us how to function on the outside but not how to follow our hearts. Then Davies takes the mic on ‘Bloody Well Right’ as the bitter grown-up who agrees your schooling is phony and shrugs. Life’s hard. Deal with it.

Back-to-back on ‘Crime of the Century’, they aren’t two songs about education. They’re an argument. One shows the machine from the inside; the other is the payoff, sung by someone who considers themselves on the right side of the line.

Fifty years on, that machine hasn’t shut down. It just changed its accent. Swap the blazers for legacy admissions, unpaid internships and postal codes. Conformity still gets rewarded, and those at the top still sound certain they earned what they were handed. They almost certainly vote ‘CONservative’, smug in their assertion that if you just work harder good things will come.

My favourite moment brings us back to the human element. Roger Hodgson’s daughter offered a tribute, recalling a kind, bearded man at the dinner table. Down-to-earth. Eternally relatable.

Close your eyes, breathe, and let that piano introduction wash over you. Then listen to the words again. Rick and Roger were trying to warn us. Millions sang along, yet few seemed to heed them.

I say it again, many speak. So, few really listen.

2. Uncle John’s Band

> [Uncle John’s Band – Ain’t No Time to Hate. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #GratefulDead#RobertHunter](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/23/uncle-johns-band-aint-no-time-to-hate-musicislife-tedtockscovers-gratefuldead-roberthunter/)

There are a million ways to slice this wonderful track from ‘Workingman’s Dead’ so I was pleased to receive this comment from Ted Tocks friend, Jim in Florida.

> Nice post, Ted as you discussed every aspect of this song. I think ‘Uncle John’s Band’ is about making an individual choice, as it says, “Come with me or go alone”, but it is open to many different interpretations, and this is probably why this song is over-analyzed so much. Hunter is a storyteller and like Shakespeare, his phrases can easily be pulled out of the context of their settings and used to give meaning to various things, depending on how they are needed at any given moment. Hunter may have borrowed some lyrics from the Bible, when he wrote, “I call it beggar’s tomb”, as Jesus tells a parable about a beggar a poor man that covered with sores and longing to eat what fell from the rich man’s table,and Jesus also had a friend named Lazarus who was raised from the dead and called out of his tomb.Hunter had varied reading habits, and he may have taken some lyrics from the‘Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam’(Persia, c. 1120) which says, “I came like Water, and like Wind I go.” Hunter wrote, “Like the morning sun you come and like the wind you go.”

I love the interaction almost as much as I love the interpretation and the fact that we can sit around and reflect on the words and wisdom of Robert Hunter and the music of the Grateful Dead.

Thanks Jim!

1. Poor Poor Pitiful Me

> [Poor Poor Pitiful Me – A Candid Revelation from the Seedy Side of Life. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #WarrenZevon#LindaRonstadt](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/07/poor-poor-pitiful-me-a-candid-revelation-from-the-seedy-side-of-life-musicislife-tedtockscovers-warrenzevon-lindaronstadt/)

I opened this feature by suggesting that ‘Poor Poor Pitiful Me’ is Warren Zevon in a nutshell. It’s a self-mocking song that grins through misfortune while taunting death, and I argue that nobody turned pain and disaster into dark comedy quite like Zevon did. This is why Warren Zevon is songwriter #3 on my Mount Rushmore of lyricists. Top marks to any Ted Tocks Covers reader who can identify the man who rounds out this esteemed list.

This feature traces the wild road that culminated in his 1976 self-titled album. Zevon had already burned through a failed record deal and scraped by as a jingle writer and touring keyboardist. Alcoholism shadowed roughly half his life, and he cheerfully described himself as deeply anti-social. Jackson Browne produced the comeback record, and the song’s mix of suicide, domestic abuse and sadomasochism was hardly typical rock fare. Zevon refused to dissect his lyrics.

Linda Ronstadt made ‘Poor Poor Pitiful Me’ a hit, reaching #31 on the Billboard chart with her ‘Simple Dreams’ version. She approached the seedier verses warily, so she and Browne reworked one from a female point of view. She saw the song as the purest expression of male vanity. The hit validated Zevon and showcased a circle of admirers who stuck with him despite his unpredictable, often toxic behaviour.

My heart overflows in the closing. Zevon died in 2003, just weeks after ‘The Wind’ arrived, at only 56. More than twenty years on, his absence still stings. Few writers combine his melodic brilliance, his blood-drawing wit and his willingness to be honest about his own flaws. He made a remarkable final album after his terminal diagnosis, joked with David Letterman about outlasting Jim Morrison, and left the advice to enjoy every sandwich. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame recently honoured him (finally). As Dawes’ Taylor Goldsmith notes, Zevon showed that you can laugh at everything and still hold it sacred.

Yes…”Enjoy every sandwich.”

> [La Grange – Just let me know if you wanna go #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #ZZTop #DustyHill #BillyGibbons #Frank Beard #JohnLeeHooker #SlimHarpo #DollyParton #BuddyHolly #KingoftheHill #TheDrewCareyShow #Slash #HankWilliamsJr #CharlieBrownandthePeanutsGang #DarylHall](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2021/08/14/la-grange-just-let-me-know-if-you-wanna-go-musicislife-tedtockscovers-zztop-dustyhill-billygibbons-frank-beard-johnleehooker-slimharpo-dollyparton-buddyholly-kingofthehill-thedrewcareysh/)

Frank Beard passed away on August 17, 2026, at his ranch in Richmond, Texas. He was 77. Beard had been ZZ Top’s drummer since the band formed in Houston in 1969. Sadly, the band and the music world lost one of rock’s most underrated timekeepers. There may be no better way to remember him than through ‘La Grange’, the 1973 track that turned ‘That Little Ol’ Band from Texas’ into a household name.

‘La Grange’ is famous for Billy Gibbons’ buzzing guitar riff, borrowed and stretched from John Lee Hooker’s boogie style, and for its cheeky lyrics about a Texas brothel known as the Chicken Ranch. But underneath all that swagger sits Beard, doing something drummers in blues-rock bands rarely get room to do; showing off, just a little.

Most bands of that era saved the flashy stuff for the arena-rock ritual, that moment mid-concert when the singer walks around introducing the band and everyone gets their sixty seconds to shine. ZZ Top never really leaned into that concert norm. But on ‘La Grange’, Beard gets about as close as the band ever came to a drum solo without technically calling it one. He doesn’t stop the song to show off. Instead, he worked his whole kit into the groove itself.

Listen closely to the opening seconds. Before Gibbons’ guitar even kicks in, Beard is already there, tapping out small, ticky-tack percussion that sounds almost like a countdown. It’s restrained, almost teasing, and it builds a sense that something bigger is coming. Then the band locks in, and Beard shifts gears completely, pounding out a rock-steady shuffle to anchor Gibbons’ electrified riffing and Dusty Hill’s rumbling bass. He’s not just keeping time. He’s finding a job for nearly every piece of his kit, moving between cymbals, snare, and toms in a way that makes the song feel like it’s constantly building even as it never strays from that hypnotic boogie pattern.

That’s the trick of ‘La Grange’, and it exemplifies Beard’s whole career. He wasn’t a drummer who called attention to himself with jaw dropping fills or spinning stick tricks. He was a groove player, someone who made three-piece blues-rock sound massive by knowing exactly when to hold back and when to cut loose. His work on ‘La Grange’ captures both sides of that talent in under four minutes.

Fifty-plus years later, with Beard gone, that song stands as one of the clearest examples of why he mattered. He didn’t need a spotlight moment. He built the spotlight into the song itself.

Next up is ‘Light of a Clear Blue Morning’ by the legendary Dolly Parton.

There is a sad irony to the fact that Ted Tocks had ‘La Grange’ cued up for this monthly piece, and it makes mention of the ‘Chicken Ranch’ and the ‘Best Little Whorehouse in Texas’ which by extension leads to the remarkable Dolly Parton. A little more than a week later I was stunned to hear the news that she had departed.

[Video 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RfinvuRolR0)

Since mainstream media has failed us so completely, I have transitioned to several podcasts in order to keep up with the news cycle. Among my favourites is ‘I’ve Had It’ with Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan. When the extremely sad news came down that Dolly Parton died on August 25, Jennifer described Dolly Parton using this phrase.

> Radical empathy.”

Perfect.

There will be more on Dolly Parton later in this post, but let it be said here that if more people in this world were like Dolly, we would not be in the quagmire we find ourselves navigating, so as I share this brief homage to Dolly Parton, I will use ‘Light of a Clear Blue Morning’ as a message hope.

Through this song Dolly Parton was hoping we could heal. ‘Light of a Clear Blue Morning’ hits harder than almost anything else in her massive catalog.

The track opens her 1977 album ‘New Harvest…First Gathering’. Almost a half century ago, it marked a turning point both musically and personally. She had just split from Porter Wagoner, her longtime musical partner and the man who had helped build her into a star. The breakup was messy, public, and painful. Parton has said she wrote this song while working through that fallout, and it shows. The lyrics describe getting through a “long dark night” and finally seeing daylight on the other side.

> I’ve been like a captured eagle,  
> You know, an eagle’s born to fly  
> Now that I, I’ve won my freedom  
> Like an eagle, I am eager for the sky”

In many ways, this is where we reside as a global community right now.

The real magic of this song is in the fact that she doesn’t wallow in misery. Instead, Parton uses the image of a sunrise as a promise that things are about to get better. ‘Light of a Clear Blue Morning’ may never get mentioned in the same breath as ‘Jolene’ or ‘I Will Always Love You’. But for pure, honest songwriting, it might be the most beautiful thing Dolly Parton ever put to paper or pressed to vinyl.

I will begin by thanking my family and guiding light for banding together behind the scenes and getting me tickets to see Rush in Toronto on Tuesday August 11 th.

My oldest son Sebastian was the lucky recipient of the second ticket. Sebastian has spent a lot of 32 plus years absorbing Rush by osmosis and he openly states that his absolute indoctrination was watching Neil Peart play the drums at the Toronto SARS festival. In the present day, Sebastian performs admirably as a drummer for at least four bands in the Peterborough area.

As the concert day approached, we made plans to converge upon the city from opposite directions. I headed over from my home in Burlington. Heather sent me off, encouraging me to blast Rush from my car as I peeled out of the court. With ‘Tom Sawyer’ blaring, I was on my way.

I knew I would be hearing it again that evening. The question was where in the set it would appear. I’ll come back to that.

We met by Union Station at the corner of Bay and Front. From there we made our way across to SkyDome. Sebastian had let me know that the Toronto Blue Jays had recently unveiled a Joe Carter statue that commemorated his game winning 1993 World Series home run. The statue also lists the outstanding team that shared in the second of back-to-back World Series victories. It took me back. Pretty special.

Next up. Time to eat and the best part is we had time to kill. Relax. Chill. We had decided on a Mexican place over on The Esplanade called 3 Mariachis. Just taking it easy for a change was a nice feeling and spending time with Sebastian added to the moment. Above and beyond, the underlying anticipation of what the evening would bring added to the experience.

As the clockwork angels moved the hour hand toward 7:30 pm we headed past St. Lawrence Market and back up to Front Street and across to the venue. During the short walk I took the time to fire a message off to my cousin Christopher. He and his son Rowan were also in town for the show. I hit send and hoped that this would not be one of those times that the recipient did not see the message until the next day. Within seconds Christopher got back to me. They were making their way down from the Massey Hall area. We made plans to connect once we were both at the venue and despite the growing throng at Gate 3 we made this happen before they opened the doors. We were able to spend about 20 minutes together before the show started.

You know that line from ’Time Stand Still’?

> Summer’s going fast  
> Nights growing colder  
> Children growing up  
> Old friends growing older”

Through a combination of circumstance, busy schedules and distance Christopher and I have not seen each other in several years. Elements of the family connection have flowed through the annals of Ted Tocks Covers on several occasions. Back in 1982 when I saw Rush for the first time, our group included my cousin Shannon; Christopher’s sister. I also haven’t seen her in too long.

Time stand still…Please…Freeze…

Anyway, despite a six-year age difference Christopher and I have a very similar taste in music and through the years some of the nicest comments about Ted Tocks features have come from Christopher’s direction. Like me, he is a natural empath who feels music. His ability to cope with the enormous challenges life throws one’s way through song has served him well. One of the positive aspects of social media is the ability to stay connected through messages and passing commentary, but nothing beats real human connection.

As showtime approached we went to our respective seats, but not before arranging to meet during the intermission.

From our vantage point Sebastian and I had a birds-eye view of the entire venue. We drank in the atmosphere as the minute hand hit the bottom of the clock. The anticipation was palpable. We took our cue from the side stage concert attendees who noted the arrival of Loren Gold and Anika Nilles and as the lights dimmed the arena roared as one. The raucous audience was treated to ‘Xanahaus’; a zany short depicting a youthful trio on a quest to find the immortal Geddy and Alex in the hopes of sharing in at least one jam session. When they finally manage to find the aged friends, they become part of a touching scene. Two longtime friends playing ‘Go Fish’ while coping with the limitations of their advanced years. Subtleties matter, and the bottle of The Macallan on the table and an empty chair still chokes me up as a type.

From here the time machine unwinds and we were taken back through a powerful montage of images of Rush through the years before everything gave way to ‘Xanadu’, the timeless track from ‘A Farewell to Kings ‘which I have noted on several occasions was the beginning of not only my Rush album collection, but also my entire collection of vinyl, cassettes, CDs and well, you get it.

Here is a Ted Tocks account of how it all went down. This goes way back to the early days of this blog.

On this night, the best way to conclude it all was to go all the way back to the beginning and so they did.

> It seems to me I could live my life

Imagine a time when they were putting in time like 9 to 5ers. Unsure. Full of doubt. But somehow prevailing on a daily basis until each day the fruits of their labour began to reveal itself to not only them, but to a circle of fans that began to expand by neighbourhood, then city then province, country, continent and globe.

Rush has always put in the work.

Has there ever been a more honest act?

Integrity has never been compromised with Rush.

Before I conclude here are a few more thoughts.

If there is an unsung hero or best supporting actor on this night the award goes to Loren Gold. In many ways, he set the table. Mostly for Geddy I suspect. That is the part that is tricky to quantify, but in short, the result was Geddy Lee at his finest. When you listen to Loren’s contribution to ‘La Villa Strangiato’ or his introduction to ‘The Camera Eye’ the value becomes immediately apparent. Know your role and stay within it. That is Loren Gold, whose musical resume is jaw dropping. Explore on your own.

What more can be said about Anika Nilles? She learned every song from the ground up and played them with power and precision. She stepped into a role where scrutinizing eyes had the potential to be unkind. She was not only flawless, but funny. She was not only professional but poised. She is and forever will be a beloved chapter of Rush because she embraced the role. This show could not have happened without her.

Once again, Geddy Lee needs to be praised for elevating himself to unimaginable heights as a performer. Typical of Geddy, he deflects any praise by pointing to his bandmates and a behind the scenes character who helped him find even more. Here is Geddy;

> His name is Mitch Seekins, and he’s a terrific guy. He’s a great singer, lives in the country now, and that’s his job. He coaches all kinds of people. It’s really interesting. He coaches opera people. He coaches a lot of rock bands. He coaches one guy who does the play-by-play announcement at a horse racetrack. So, all kinds of people need vocal training, for various [reasons]… He coaches people that, for one reason or another, have started to lose their voice. And so he’s very well-versed in analyzing what you got. So, I started with him — what? — about a year and a half ago now. And the first few sessions, he was listening to what I had, and he said, ‘Okay. Well, you’ve got a voice that the muscles are out of shape. So you haven’t sung in 11 years. That’s normal.’ So, after the first number of sessions, he said, ‘Well, the good news is you still have that range in there, but we’ve gotta strengthen your voice so you can access it.”

Hats off to Mitch.

On this night I was sitting on Alex’s side, so I spent a lot of time watching him play. He is having the time of his life. The interaction between him and his bandmates is a sight to behold. His solos flow and the audience is with him on every note. Sure, there were some moments where the fingers were not cooperating the way he would have liked. Shortly after the harmonics on Red Barchetta did not come across as crisp as he would have liked he delivered ‘YYZ’, ‘Limelight’ and his stunning parts on ‘The Camera Eye’ like he was 27 again. The resilience and the resolve is remarkable. Best of all, he handles every second of this magical tour with his trademark sense of humour. Alex defines cool. He is like every Rush fans cool older brother.

Figuring out a way to conclude this piece is tricky, so I will focus on the fan base. Rush fans are coming out in droves for this tour. They are enjoying every second. It is fun to watch, and honestly, I can’t believe it is happening at all. This is bonus time, and it is full value.

Geddy and Alex did not undertake this project without a lot of thought and painstaking consideration. They have been very open about the decision-making process. In some ways this is their gift to millions of devoted fans, but this is also them proving to themselves that they are not older, they are better.

Like Geddy Lee said;

> I never thought I would see this again. Thank you for that.”

Exit…Stage Left on night three of ‘Fifty Something’ at ‘Corporate Surcharge’ Arena. Rush used to call themselves three hosers from Canada, a self-deprecating little joke from a band that never took itself too seriously even while writing some of the most complex music ever recorded. That joke hits different in August 2026. There’s noise coming from south of the border these days, talk of Canada as some 51st state, and Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson didn’t need to say a word about it. They just played. For two and a half hours, in their hometown, with Neil Peart’s face on the screen behind them and his spirit all over every fill Anika Nilles played, Rush stood as living proof of something specific and something Canadian. This band survived tragedy, survived eleven years of silence, survived the kind of loss that ends most bands for good. And they came back anyway, on their own terms, in their ‘hometown’.

So, when they say they’ve assumed control, believe it. Rush isn’t touring for nostalgia. They’re touring because the world needs reminding that some things don’t get absorbed, don’t get bought out, don’t get renamed.

As I type, ‘Tears’ are welling up from deep inside.

> What would touch me deeper  
> Tears that fall from eyes that only cry?  
> Would it touch you deeper  
> Than tears that fall from eyes that know why?”

Long live Rush!

Ted Tocks tradition has come to dictate that I pay my respect to artists or significant musical figures who left us over the past month.

Music lost one of its greatest visionaries in June. Clive Davis died at the age 94 at his Manhattan home. Davis didn’t just sign artists, he built eras. From 1967 to 1973, as president of Columbia Records, he pulled a tired, jazz-and-Broadway label into the rock age, betting on Janis Joplin, Santana, and a driven young New Jersey kid named Bruce Springsteen.

Yes, there was a scandal. He was pushed out of Columbia in 1973 over allegations of misusing corporate funds. He pleaded guilty to tax evasion. Most careers would have ended there but Clive’s didn’t. He turned a collection of failing labels into Arista Records, and that’s where his legend really grew. He gave Barry Manilow his first chart-topper with ‘Mandy’ then found a teenager named Whitney Houston singing in a New York nightclub, and turned her into one of the best-selling pop artists in music history. He also helped revive careers that had stalled out. The list includes Dionne Warwick, Rod Stewart, Aretha Franklin, and even the Grateful Dead, who he brought to Arista in the ’70s. Deadheads loved him so much that Bob Weir once swapped a ‘Jack Straw’ lyric in concert to,

> Now we play for Clive.”

Here you go.

[Video 26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UezKUqVFhxc)

His ear never stopped working. He launched Alicia Keys in 2001, shaped the sound coming off ‘American Idol’, and kept hosting his legendary pre-Grammy party which was known as the hottest ticket in music. This event took place right up until this year’s edition in January.

Bruce Springsteen called him a “great record man and close friend.” Patti Smith thanked him for “transforming music.” That’s the real measure of Clive Davis. Artists across six decades, from Joplin to Jelly Roll, all saying the same thing. To a person they will tell you, he heard something in them before anyone else did.

Two days after we learned of Clive Davis’s death news of David Clayton-Thomas’s passing came over the news streams. When we talk about bands that blurred the lines between rock, jazz, and soul, the conversation has to start with Blood, Sweat & Tears, and more specifically, with the gravel-voiced Canadian who fronted them through their commercial peak. That was David Clayton-Thomas.

Blood Sweat & Tears didn’t just dabble in horns. They built an entire musical landscape around them. Trumpets, trombones, saxophones were stacked and swinging with the precision of a big band, but driven by a rhythm section that understood the rock ‘n roll pulse and the soul groove. This wasn’t just novelty. It was a genuine attempt to widen what a rock band could sound like, and it worked spectacularly on their self-titled 1969 album. They would go on to sweep the Grammys, giving us ‘Spinning Wheel’ (shared at the outset) and ‘You’ve Made Me So Very Happy’.

[Video 27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fcvXDuBruSQ)

As well as a cover of Laura Nyro’s magnificent ‘And When I Die’.

> [And When I Die – Sometimes by going deep inside the music we gain the strength to carry on. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #LauraNyro #PeterPaulandMary #BloodSweatandTears #DuaneAllman #TennesseeErnieFord #JuniorWalkerandtheAllStars](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2022/04/08/and-when-i-die-sometimes-by-going-deep-inside-the-music-we-gain-the-strength-to-carry-on-musicislife-tedtockscovers-lauranyro-peterpaulandmary-bloodsweatandtears-duaneallman-tennesse/)

David Clayton-Thomas was the engine. His voice had the rasp of blues, the phrasing of jazz, and the power of soul. It was capable of belting like a horn section himself. He didn’t just sing over the arrangements; he matched their complexity, riding time signature shifts and key changes without losing the emotional thread.

What makes Blood Sweat & Tears significant isn’t just that they mixed genres, because plenty of bands sampled jazz chords or blended in a horn line. It’s that they treated jazz and soul as equal structural partners to rock. They share that distinction with acts like Chicago and Tower of Power, but Blood Sweat & Tears arguably got there first with that level of ambition, and Clayton-Thomas’s voice gave it a rock-and-roll grit that made the fusion feel urgent rather than stuffy.

Their influence echoes anywhere a band reaches for horns instead of a guitar solo. This becomes a reminder that genre lines were always more malleable than the radio dial suggested.

3. Beautiful Things

> [Beautiful Things – Flipping Out Over Benson Boone. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers#BensonBoone](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/06/25/beautiful-things-flipping-out-over-benson-boone-musicislife-tedtockscovers-bensonboone/)

This feature opens with a confession. For the first half of my 50 years of music fandom I was guilty of dismissing every new trend, from punk to boy bands. But over the last quarter century I have learned to be more accepting of a wide range of styles and genres as well as emerging new artists. Benson Boone is among this group.

Early in this feature I allude to Boone’s Coachella duet with Brian May on ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’, a moment that proved Boone could more than hold his own next to a rock legend. From there, my focus shifts to ‘Beautiful Things’ which was Boone’s breakout hit, topping the charts in over 20 countries.

From acceptance, the real story is how the song came together. Boone wrote it over two separate nights, producing two unrelated song fragments. Songwriter Jack LaFrantz suggested mashing them into one track, an idea that changed everything. Here I draw comparisons to The Beatles stitching together “A Day in the Life” from leftover Lennon-McCartney scraps, and Taylor Swift building “Getaway Car” from two clashing concepts with Jack Antonoff.

More happy accidents followed. Producer Evan Blair’s pedal mistakenly distorted the guitar tone, and instead of fixing it, Boone kept it. The two halves of the song were even written in different time signatures, taking two weeks to blend properly.

‘Beautiful Things’ has some beautiful symbolism too. The mountaintop music video symbolizes both triumph and the fear of falling, and Boone’s raw, shirtless vocal take captured genuine anguish rather than performance.

2. I Just Wasn’t Made for These Times

> [I Just Wasn’t Made for These Times – Sometimes I Feel Very Sad. Compassion Fatigue Has Set In. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #BrianWilson#TheBeachBoys](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/06/11/i-just-wasnt-made-for-these-times-sometimes-i-feel-very-sad-compassion-fatigue-has-set-in-musicislife-tedtockscovers-brianwilson-thebeachboys/)

I dive into ‘I Just Wasn’t Made for These Times’ because, out of everything Brian Wilson ever wrote, this song feels like the truest window into who he was. Co-written with Tony Asher and built with help from the legendary Wrecking Crew, the track features an unusual bass line using thirds instead of root notes, a haunting Electro-Theremin solo, and layered vocals that wrap around Wilson’s confession like voices in his own head. I lean on John Cale’s famous line from the 1995 Don Was documentary that gave the song its title;

> There was something genuine in every lyric Wilson wrote, and that honesty could be a burden.”

Wilson admitted outright that the song was about himself, about feeling “too advanced” for his own time while making ‘Pet Sounds’ in 1966, even as friends doubted him. Placed near the album’s end, after the worn-down hope of ‘[Wouldn’t It Be Nice](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/01/22/wouldnt-it-be-nice-to-live-in-the-kind-of-world-where-we-all-belong-musicislife-tedtockscovers-thebeachboys-brianwilson-tonyasher/)’ and the ache of ‘God Only Knows’ the song becomes a kind of confession booth, a place where Wilson finally admits he doesn’t fit in anywhere.

From this truth I manage to pull that loneliness into today’s world. I argue that feeling out of step with the world isn’t just Wilson’s story anymore, it’s ours. Between social media comparison, widening inequality, and constant outrage, I suggest we’re all dealing with a kind of compassion fatigue, growing numb to suffering because there’s simply too much of it. Wilson wasn’t writing about any of that specifically, but great art works like a mirror.

I close out with a tour of covers, from Aimee Mann and Michael Penn to Jim James and Jakob Dylan with Neil Young, plus a nod to that unforgettable ‘Mad Men’ needle-drop. I end the piece reflecting on Wilson’s passing on June 11, 2025, exactly one year before this was written, urging readers to put on headphones, really listen, and realize his music still keeps us company.

1. I Want to Make You Higher

> [I Want to Take You Higher – It’s a Musical Conversation. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #SlyandtheFamilyStone #SlyStone](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/06/09/i-want-to-take-you-higher-its-a-musical-conversation-musicislife-tedtockscovers-slyandthefamilystone-slystone/)

My goal here was to tell you about a song that started small and ended up changing history. ‘I Want to Take You Higher’ by Sly and the Family Stone didn’t begin in 1969, it traces back to 1966, when Sly Stone wrote a tune called ‘Advice’ for Billy Preston. That song barely made a dent on the charts, but Sly kept tinkering with it. By 1968 he’d formed his own band, a group that was both racially and gender mixed at a time when American cities were literally burning with race riots. They reworked ‘Advice’ into a song called ‘Higher’. Then in 1969, with the album ‘Stand’ they rebuilt it again, adding a blazing guitar riff and a horn section. There it was, tucked it away as a B-side. It barely cracked the Top 60.

Then came Woodstock. Between 3:30 and 4:20 am, after a brutal rainstorm, with half a million exhausted people sitting in the mud, Sly Stone walked out and asked the crowd to sing with him. They answered back with one word, shouted over and over:

> Higher”

That moment turned a forgotten B-side into one of the most legendary performances in music history.

What makes the song so powerful is its use of call and response, a tradition rooted in African music, carried through slavery, and built into gospel churches. Sly grew up Pentecostal, so this wasn’t a gimmick to him; it was church, just with funk instead of hymns. The song’s simplicity is the genius part. Anyone can shout ‘Higher’ so the whole crowd becomes part of the band.

Sly Stone passed away one year ago, but his message of unity through music still hits hard. Nearly 60 years later, that one word still gets people to answer back.
