# [Battle Scar – Remembering the Poet Behind the Power. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #MaxWebster #PyeDubois #Rush #NeilPeart#KimMitchell](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/03/battle-scar-remembering-the-poet-behind-the-power-musicislife-tedtockscovers-maxwebster-pyedubois-rush-neilpeart-kimmitchell/)

[October 3, 2026 October 3, 2026](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/03/battle-scar-remembering-the-poet-behind-the-power-musicislife-tedtockscovers-maxwebster-pyedubois-rush-neilpeart-kimmitchell/) ~ [tedlindsay0170](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/author/tedlindsay0170/) ~ [Leave a comment](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/03/battle-scar-remembering-the-poet-behind-the-power-musicislife-tedtockscovers-maxwebster-pyedubois-rush-neilpeart-kimmitchell/#respond)

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PMM6Bhwpy0M)

Some songwriters never stand behind a microphone, yet their words echo as loud as the people singing them.

I am thinking of writers like Robert Hunter, Bernie Taupin, Shel Silverstein, Peter Sinfield and Norman Whitfield. I could go on. It’s a fascinating subject because they are stars in every right, but rarely did they accept the spotlight.

Pye Dubois is one of those writers. Most casual fans know Dubois from ‘Tom Sawyer’, clearly his most recognizable song.

> [Tom Sawyer – A monumental track from Moving Pictures by Rush and a few personal reflections. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #Rush #NeilPeart #PyeDubois #Alex Lifeson #GeddyLee #AlexisonFire #TenaciousD #StringCheeseIncident #JackBlack#ImagineDragons](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2019/09/12/tom-sawyer-a-monumental-track-from-moving-pictures-by-rush-and-a-few-personal-reflections-musicislife-tedtockscovers-rush-neilpeart-pyedubois-alex-lifeson-geddylee-alexisonfire-tenaciousd/)

But if you want to understand what made Dubois special, you must dig a little deeper, and Battle Scar’ is a perfect place to start.

Here is where I should add some context. Pye Dubois was a Canadian poet and lyricist who wrote for every Max Webster album. Over roughly two decades he also collaborated with Neil Peart on four Rush songs. In addition to his contribution to ‘Tom Sawyer’ he co-wrote ‘Force 10’ from ‘Hold Your Fire’.

> We can rise and fall like empires  
> Flow in and out like the tide  
> Be vain and smart, humble and dumb  
> We can hit-and-miss like pride  
> Just like pride  
> We can circle around like hurricanes  
> Dance and dream like lovers  
> Attack the day like birds of prey  
> Or scavengers under cover, under cover”

Imagine; this was written almost forty years ago.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NS1lbRU0Fzw)

Then there was ‘Between Sun and Moon’ from ‘Counterparts’.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zsfgewRxwu8)

More on that album in a bit.

Then there was ‘Test for Echo’ the title track from Rush’s sixteenth studio album.

> Some kind of pictures on the sense o’clock news  
> Miles of yellow tape, silhouetted chalk lines  
> Tough-talking hood boys in pro-team logo knock-offs  
> Conform to uniforms of some corporate entity  
> Don’t change that station  
> It’s a Gangsta Nation  
> Now crime’s in syndication on TV”

One decade later, and Pye Dubois and Neil Peart effortless capture the present and predict the future all at once.

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=deUirMqTV6A)

His partner in Max Webster; the band’s front man Kim Mitchell, described his contribution in this way.

> You sure knew how to jam with the English language and bring it!

Dubois didn’t hand you a neat narrative. He handed you a canvas and trusted you to feel what was on it. In 2021, Dubois and Mitchell were inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame, which says plenty about how far his influence reached.

‘Battle Scar’ might be the finest example of this talent at full strength. It is a gripping, dramatic piece, and it sounds even bigger because Rush lent their epic talent to the recording. Geddy Lee’s unmistakable voice and the band’s precision give the track a weight that matches its subject matter. But the music is only half the story. The real power is in the lyrics.

What makes ‘Battle Scar’ so alluring is how it treats human conflict. Dubois doesn’t write a flag-waving anthem or a simple ‘war is bad’ slogan. Instead, he looks across a millennium of human history and suggests that over time, the violence has left marks that never fully heal. Figuratively, that scar becomes the central image of the song. A wound closes, but the mark remains as proof of what happened. Applied to humanity, that idea is chilling. Every generation inherits the scars of the ones before it, and sadly, we keep adding new ones.

This is why the song works as a veiled protest. It is way more than a hard rock anthem. Protest music is often direct and loud, but Dubois builds his statement through imagery and atmosphere. The lyrics move through scenes of conflict, conquest, and suffering without pinning themselves to a single war or era. That approach is brilliant. Because the song isn’t tied to one event, it can speak to many. Within the economy of words, we are taken to ancient battlefields, modern conflicts, and every atrocity in between. A listener in 1980, and a listener today can both find their own world inside it. The song accuses humanity of a crime. Allowing history to repeat itself, and it does so without ever lecturing.

If you are a fan of Max Webster and Rush, tell me…Did you know ‘Battle Scar’ was a history lesson baked into a power rock jam?

Within this context there is a sense of grief running underneath. The song doesn’t celebrate victors. It lingers on the cost, on the people who carry the damage long after the fighting stops. That emotional honesty is part of why the track hits so hard, even for listeners who can’t quite explain what the words mean. Like Neil Peart’s masterpiece ‘Bravado’ from ‘Roll the Bones’ you feel the weight before you decode the poetry.

> And if the music stops, there’s only the sound of the rain  
> All the hope and glory, all the sacrifice in vain”

We WILL pay the price.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUSpBAmSMb8)

These are the themes that run through the lyrical journey that Pye Dubois delivered. His wider career elaborates on this instinct. His poem ‘There Is a Lake Between Sun and Moon’ inspired Rush to write many of the lyrics for the album ‘Counterparts’.

> There is a lake between sun and moon  
> Not too many know about  
> Some go there for their high noon  
> Some go there for their midnight moon  
> It is a moment between silence and shout  
> Maybe you, might as well me  
> Why the sun, why the sun  
> Say yes, say yes, ahh say yes to self-esteem  
> We want to escape because we don’t want to fall in  
> The signs are clear and so is the fear  
> We do not trust the firmness of the ground  
> Then say yes, say yes, ahh say yes to self-esteem  
> There is a fine place between actor and audience  
> This is the fine line  
> The fine line of living  
> This moment experienced  
> This fine deliverance  
> Do what you want to do in no ordinary way  
> Say what you need to say in no ordinary way  
> And sing what must be sung in no ordinary way  
> Say yes, ahh please, please say yes to self-esteem  
> Some go there for their high noon  
> Some go there for their midnight moon  
> It is the moment between silent and shout  
> This is a fine place  
> Faces face to face  
> These bonfire eyes  
> In the lake of the sky  
> It is our light to land and leave  
> Never so dark to unravel the weave  
> Never give up and never say die  
> Do what you need to do in no ordinary way  
> Say what you need to say in no ordinary way  
> And sing what must be sung in no ordinary way”

A poem inspiring a whole album tells you how rich and flexible his imagery was. Many writers supplied stories; Dubois offered the spark that lit the fire.

Looking back, his significance is clear. He proved that rock lyrics in their brevity could be literature, never losing their punch. He showed that a song can protest the worst parts of human history while still being thrilling to listen to. And in ‘Battle Scar’, he left us a reminder that the past never really leaves us, because we not only wear it, but we perpetuate the atrocities through crimes of commission and omission.

That is the mark of a great songwriter. Pye Dubois wrote words that make you think, make you feel, and perhaps most importantly, they make you want to hit replay.

As long as the music is playing, maybe the moral will penetrate our collective mind by osmosis?

Back to its origin, ‘Battle Scar’ was recorded live in studio in July of 1980, and released as the closing track on side one of ‘Universal Juveniles’ on this day 46 years ago.

The scorching album track was recorded at Phase One Studios in Toronto. Present at the session were members of Max Webster including Terry Watkinson on keyboards, and of course Geddy, Alex and Neil from Rush. The friendship between Rush and Max Webster went way back. Here is Kim Mitchell discussing the friendship that began just over 50 years ago when the members of Max Webster arrived in Toronto, making their way from their Sarnia roots.

> Rush were great friends and they always treated us as equals. There were so many beautiful moments, and they made touring so enjoyable. I can still picture Neil with a book and a pack of cigarettes. He was an intense dude, but so sweet once you knew him. I remember one day Alex couldn’t make sound-check, and I played with Ged and Neil.”

Max Webster’s debut album was released in May of 1976 on Rush manager Ray Danniels’s Taurus label. It was co-produced by long time Rush producer, Terry Brown. The close connection led to many live shows featuring Rush as the headliner and Max Webster as the supporting act.

Although the friendship was genuine, added importance could be found in Rush’s role as mentors as to how to survive in the music industry. Again, here is Kim Mitchell.

> Rush taught us that you should make your own decisions and not listen to record company bullshit. They were like, ‘This is our music, and these are our lives.”

By 1979 Max Webster had hit their commercial peak but at the same time they became victims of the harshness of the music industry. Following the success of ‘A Million Vacations’ the band’s U.S. label, refused to fund a European tour which would have seen the band headline. By the middle of 1980, Max Webster was determined to show Capitol they had made a mistake. They brought former Guess Who producer, Jack Richardson on board to work on the material that would become ‘Universal Juveniles’.

Among the collection of great songs was a demo for ‘Battle Scar.

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TP2sQEeVMuk)

All of this led to the two bands coming together on that summer day 46 years ago to create this relentless musical attack where every player fed off each other to create multiple layers of musical greatness. If you ever need a song to motivate you, this is it…

> Been in jail for a thousand years  
> Found a fist in an empty field  
> Only quarters for meals  
> Feel the way I feel  
>   
> Bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel  
>   
> Tried to understand the white man’s fears  
> Make ’em bend but they wouldn’t yield  
> Uncle Sam’s time is only a greased wheel  
> Feel the way I feel  
>   
> Bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel  
> I said bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel”

It borders on tragic that this would become Max Webster’s final studio album, but without the support from their label things slowly disintegrated. Kim Mitchell opted to leave the band in April of 1981 following a gig in Nashville. Was it fitting or sad that on this day Max Webster was the opening act for Rush?

For a quality take on the circumstances that led to ‘Battle Scar’ and the ‘Universal Juveniles’ album check out this excellent article from ‘Norseland’s Rock’.

> [THE STORY BEHIND THE SONG: «Battle Scar» by Max Webster and Rush](https://norselandsrock.com/battle-scar-max-webster-rush/)

Now, let’s look back at ‘Battle Scar’ through the years. Kim Mitchell had a successful solo career and much of his success can be attributed to his charisma and an always upbeat live show. That show always included ‘Battle Scar’ as an electrifying set closer. Here is Kim Mitchell out on the road in 1990.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YcnHH74p95w)

This is a real treat. Let’s go back to the 14 th Annual Andy Kim Christmas Show in December of 2018. Watch and listen as Alex joins Kim Mitchell and his band, but before we do, here is Alex speaking on the friendship between Rush and Max Webster and his memories of Pye Dubois.

> Those guys were big friends of ours. But Pye was a little mysterious – kind of a strange fellow! He was very quirky, a bit of a nut, but he did write great lyrics.”

Personal connections brought together through music are rarely forgotten.

[Video 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Fa8Co3BuJ4)

My search for pure cover versions led me to this interesting cover by Tom Gordon. This is well done. It stays true to the original with just enough of the artist’s obvious talent shining through.

[Video 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0nMPArI9rpA)

Most recently we find ourselves in 2023 at the Canada’s Walk of Fame Induction Ceremony with Gordie Johnson and Charlie Edward paying tribute to Max Webster. This recognition is well deserved.

[Video 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cA9_t8fDIHE)

If the verses of ‘Battle Scar’ mourn the wounds of history, the outro is where the song stops grieving and starts demanding change, or at least some semblance of action. The closing chant is relentless. It repeats like a rally cry, and each line turns the spotlight on a different kind of power. Those who destroy are told their time is coming. Those who profit from other people’s hunger are called out. Even the healers, the people trusted to care, are challenged to feel the pain they treat from a distance.

‘Battle Scar’ is Pye Dubois at his sharpest. He doesn’t name a villain, so the target keeps shifting with the times. Today, it’s easy to hear the chant aimed at war profiteers, corporations that thrive on scarcity, and institutions that talk about caring while staying insulated from consequences. The repetition makes it feel less like a lyric and more like an angry mob. A protest building volume until it can’t be ignored.

But where are all the people?

More than forty years later, the outro still works as a warning. It reminds the powers that be that people remember who caused the scars, and who profited from them. Great protest songs outlive their moment, and Pye Dubois understood that. “Battle Scar” doesn’t fade out quietly. It begs us to act.

> Bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel  
> I said bust the busters  
> Screw the feeders  
> Make the healers  
> Feel the way I feel”

Upon Pye Dubois’ passing in September, Kim Mitchell shared his sadness with these words.

> Some say freedom is after the storm.”

True valour exists in rising to meet the challenge and inspiring people to join the fight.

Freedom is not a birthright. It has to be earned.

# [Angel Dream – His Music is With Us Everywhere We Go. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #TomPetty #TomPettyandtheHeartbreakers](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/02/angel-dream-with-us-everywhere-we-go-musicislife-tedtockscovers-tompetty-tompettyandtheheartbreakers/)

[October 2, 2026 October 1, 2026](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/02/angel-dream-with-us-everywhere-we-go-musicislife-tedtockscovers-tompetty-tompettyandtheheartbreakers/) ~ [tedlindsay0170](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/author/tedlindsay0170/) ~ [Leave a comment](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/10/02/angel-dream-with-us-everywhere-we-go-musicislife-tedtockscovers-tompetty-tompettyandtheheartbreakers/#respond)

[Video 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B8eN5F22KbA)

On this day let’s talk about the quiet little album hiding in Tom Petty’s vast catalogue.

Ask most people to name a Tom Petty album and you’ll hear ‘Damn the Torpedoes’, ‘Full Moon Fever’, or ‘Wildflowers’. Almost nobody says, ‘Songs and Music from the Motion Picture She’s the One’. That’s a shame, because this 1996 soundtrack is one of the most interesting stops in the Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers story. And the best place to start is a somewhat haunting, yet stirring song called ‘Angel Dream’.

It was so good he did it twice. ‘Angel Dream’ shows up on the record in two versions. The version this feature opened with is known as ‘Angel Dream (No. 2)’. It is the stripped-down offering, soft and intimate, like a lullaby whispered at the end of a long day. ‘Angel Dream (No. 4)’ has more of the full band in it, with a warmer, rounder sound.

[Video 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-qcL9rnkP2Y)

Hearing the same song twice, dressed differently, tells you something about how this project worked. Petty wasn’t just handing in finished singles. He was an artist at the easel, testing colour, and texture on his canvas and then stepping back to let the songs breathe.

In hindsight, the lyrics are simple on purpose. The song is about hoping someone you love finds peace, even when the world is loud and confusing.

Remarkably, the song takes on an even deeper meaning in 2026.

To his credit, Tom Petty never oversold that feeling, and that’s why it lands. In a career that lasted four full decades ‘Angel Dream’ is one of the most heartfelt lyrics he ever wrote.

This leads into the context of why the timing matters.

To see why this soundtrack is essential Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers we must recall, where Petty was in 1996. He had just made ‘Wildflowers’, a deeply personal album that many fans call his best. He was also dealing with big changes in his life and band. Longtime drummer Stan Lynch was gone, and Steve Ferrone had stepped in behind the kit. Rick Rubin, who produced ‘Wildflowers’, was still in the picture, and the mood was reflective and a little bit frayed.

> I really love making music and I love making records. We’re a much better rock ’n’ roll band than we were in 1976. The trick is to just not really let it become work. As long as it is just fun, it keeps you interested.”

Searching for fun, may have been the shift in Petty’s direction that occurred when director Edward Burns asked him to score his film about two brothers tangled between love and loyalty. Petty said yes, and the songs that came out of it feel like a bridge between ‘Wildflowers’ and whatever was to come.

It is debatable, but perhaps many would suggest that in addition to the ‘Angel Dream’ double attack the soundtrack’s biggest calling card is ‘Walls’ which like ‘Angel Dream’ appears in more than one form. ‘Walls (Circus)’ is the punchier, more radio-ready take, with a bright guitar lift that sticks in your head.

[Video 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZfS6Nl962Qg)

‘Walls (No. 3)’ slows things down and leans into the sadness under the melody.

> And all around your island  
> There’s a barricade  
> That keeps out the danger  
> That holds in the pain  
> Sometimes you’re happy  
> Sometimes you cry  
> Half of me is ocean  
> Half of me is sky”

The song is about the barriers people build around themselves, and hearing it two ways drives the point home.

[Video 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QK9ylm3ijbo)

The same feeling can come out as an indifferent shrug or as an nagging ache.

Ultimately what Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers fans discover is something they had known for two decades. The Heartbreakers was a band that could do it all. In this writer’s opinion, they are the best backing band in music history next to The Band.

What’s great about this record is how much ground it covers. “Zero from Outer Space” is a scrappy, fun rocker.

> I’ve been wrapped up in confusion  
> I’ve been tied down to my bed  
> Suffering some illusion  
> I’m out of my fuckin’ head  
> It’s insane to my brain  
> I ran away”

It also explains a lot about Tom Petty’s headspace.

[Video 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kx_E_ZCL1no)

“Climb That Hill” is a driving, road-ready track that sounds like it belongs in the car with the windows down.

> I gotta bury my pride  
> Drag this line  
> Over that hill  
> One more time  
> Gotta get up in the mornin’  
> Make my way  
> Over that hill again”

It’s like Tom Petty found “something good waiting down this road” once but then things went sour…a companion to ‘Running Down a Dream’.

[Video 16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aTSxLZWsSKs)

“Grew Up Fast” carries a story-song feel, looking back at how quickly childhood disappears.

> We grew up last  
> When lies were just a fact of life  
> Grew up mad  
> ‘Cause we never had a home  
> We faced the past  
> And forgave the revolution  
> We grew up smashed  
> And we grew up alone  
> We grew up alone”

This speaks directly to the audience that had been following him from the beginning. Listen to Benmon Tench’s piano and Mike Campbell’s guitar. A vintage song in a vast library.

[Video 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=coBgb7Ef9uo)

‘Hope You Never’ and ‘Hope on Board’ bring a hopeful, almost prayerful mood; the titles lay out the optimism. ‘Asshole’ pokes fun with a darker sense of humor and reminds you Petty could be sharp-tongued when he wanted to be.

> Your brains went black  
> When she took back her love  
> And put it out into the sun  
> The birds did fly  
> When the heavens all went dry  
> And the cigarettes were smoking by themselves”

It’s the derision that exited in the moment.

[Video 18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BIn8JRZ58Io)

“Supernatural Radio” has a dreamy, late-night glow, like tuning in to a station that only plays for you. “Hung Up and Overdue” and “Airport” add moody, wandering textures, the kind of songs that make more sense when you hear the whole record in order. And “California” gives the album a little sunshine and space.

Then there’s “Change the Locks,” a cover of a Lucinda Williams song.

[Video 19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zi4FbohLSjs)

Bitter? Maybe?

Tom Petty was always a big believer in honoring other writers, and the Heartbreakers turn it into a tough, gritty rocker. It’s a nice reminder of where Petty came from. He was a fan first, and he never forgot it. Just listen to Tom Petty Radio. It’s a never-ending music education.

Before moving on, here is Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers well known cover of ‘Thirteen Days’ by J.J. Cale.

[Video 20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vBPTP2rCzag)

This is why ‘She’s the One’ belongs in the conversation when discussing Tom Petty’s finest offerings.

Here’s the real argument for this soundtrack. Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers were often treated as a greatest hits band, a group people loved for the songs on the radio. But records like this show what they sounded like when nobody was chasing a hit. It’s all about the deep tracks. The playing is loose but tight. The songs are short, honest, and lean. Mike Campbell’s guitar-work still sparkles, Benmont Tench’s keyboards add color, and the rhythm section keeps everything steady.

Because it was a soundtrack, the pressure was lower, and that freedom shows. Petty and the band could try alternate versions, quiet moods, and side-road ideas. In a way, the album feels like a private diary that just happened to get released. Consider it Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers version of ‘The Basement Tapes’ or ‘Music from the Big Pink’

It also sits at an important moment in the timeline. After the emotional depth of ‘Wildflowers’ and before the more polished sound of ‘Echo’, this record captures Petty completely comfortable with imperfection. You can hear a songwriter who has nothing left to prove. For another comparison, consider Neil Young and ‘Tonight’s the Night’.

All of this brings is meant to bring us back to ‘Angel Dream’. Of everything on the soundtrack, it may be the one that best sums up why the album matters. It’s small, gentle, and deeply human. It doesn’t need a big chorus or a flashy solo. It just makes you feel like someone is looking out for you. No matter where you reside, in the world today we need this reminder that our best hope for coping with the shit show we have sown is a trust in each other…and the music.

So, the point is, if all you know of Tom Petty is the big radio hits, I want you to try something. Put on this album. Start with ‘Angel Dream (No. 2)’ and just let it wash over you like “waves crashing on the beach.”. Then skip ahead to ‘Walls (Circus)’ and keep going from there. For a moment you will feel less desperate. This is probably the most low-key record he ever made, and we all know Tom Petty was a laid-back dude. That’s exactly why it might sneak up on you and end up being one of your favorites.

Now on to the covers where we are greeted with a couple of country music legends. As an introduction, check out Tom’s thoughts on the country music scene, circa 1996.

> What they call country now is atrocious. What it really is, is bad rock. It was people who couldn’t cut it in rock. They’ve decided to package it as country or whatever.”

This is what connects ‘Angel Dream’ to the artists who Ted Tocks is featuring in today’s tribute.

Please ‘Meet Glen Campbell’ and his cover form the album of the same name. This was his sixtieth of Campbell’s career. Just a mindboggling number.

[Video 21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N4wXunnM8pg)

That cover was so good I needed to share the cover that followed on this recording that featured Campbell’s interpretation of several contemporary artists.

> “Some things are over  
> Some things go on  
> Part of me you carry  
> Part of me is gone”

Here is ‘Walls’.

[Video 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t9TvjirR2ZQ)

Following this special pair of covers from Glen Campbell it would take something special to match or exceed the sentimentality, but I may have met the challenge. In 2024, Willie Nelson joined his son Lukas Nelson for this cover of ‘A Country Music Celebration of Tom Petty’. When Willie sings;

> Sing a little song for loneliness  
> Sing one to make me smile  
> Another round for everyone  
> I’m here for a little while”

This is a moment for the ages. Consider this; Willie Nelson would have been 91 when he recorded this cover.

[Video 23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PH4oKqt1nGM)

That album also featured Dolly Parton’s cover of ‘Southern Accents’. Willie, Lukas and Dolly may represent the best of a very strong group of recordings.

[Video 24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e2qvHyFVm20)

Check it out when you get time.

So here we are, spinning Tom Petty as another year has gone by. Marking the ninth anniversary of Tom Petty’s passing and still finding new corners of his catalogue worth talking about. That’s the thing about Petty. He wasn’t chasing trends or trying to sound smart. He just told the truth, plain and simple, and let the songs do the rest.

‘Angel Dream’ is proof of that. It’s not flashy. It’s not trying to impress anybody. It’s just honest, the kind of song that sounds like it was already floating around somewhere, and Petty just happened to be the guy who caught it. He said it himself over the years.

> The best songs often just appear”

You don’t force them. You stay out of the way and let them show up.

That’s really the whole story of his career. Whether he was writing about heartbreak, freedom, growing up, or just some small, quiet moment of hope, he never overdressed the feeling. He trusted it. He trusted us to feel it.

That’s why his songs still hit the same way, all these years later. They weren’t built for a moment. They were built for the truth of the moment.

While we live in a world of lies, Tom Petty’s legacy may be that the truth will never go out of style. We need to be vigilant in this belief.

That’s Tom Petty. The genuine article. Authentic to the core.

Tom Petty believed.

So, on a day like today, it feels right to put on something quiet. Let “Angel Dream” play. Let it remind you that his sincerity never needed to be loud to matter.

Okay, when you turn it up, it does get even better, but I digress.

Tom Petty knew that better than almost anybody, and he left us a whole catalogue of music and the associated memories that proves it.

All of that happens one honest song at a time and Ted Tocks Covers is here to share.

Just doing my part, from the shores of Lake Ontario.

When I set down to write this feature, I was aiming to share how some songs make you stop everything and listen. ‘School’ and ‘Bloody Well Right’ still do that to me.

Is it the harmonica? The longing vocals? The piano that wanders off on its own mid-song? Or is it that so few writers today hold the establishment to account, and we need them more than ever?

In early September I marked the first anniversary of Rick Davies’ passing through these timeless Supertramp tracks. Davies’ bluesy piano is the backbone of these two tracks, but the feature reminds us that this was a partnership. Roger Hodgson brought the melody and the bruised sensitivity; Davies brought the grit.

Yin and yang.

‘School’ grew from Hodgson’s boarding school years at Stowe, a sensitive boy sent away to be made sensible. Schools, he says, teach us how to function on the outside but not how to follow our hearts. Then Davies takes the mic on ‘Bloody Well Right’ as the bitter grown-up who agrees your schooling is phony and shrugs. Life’s hard. Deal with it.

Back-to-back on ‘Crime of the Century’, they aren’t two songs about education. They’re an argument. One shows the machine from the inside; the other is the payoff, sung by someone who considers themselves on the right side of the line.

Fifty years on, that machine hasn’t shut down. It just changed its accent. Swap the blazers for legacy admissions, unpaid internships and postal codes. Conformity still gets rewarded, and those at the top still sound certain they earned what they were handed. They almost certainly vote ‘CONservative’, smug in their assertion that if you just work harder good things will come.

My favourite moment brings us back to the human element. Roger Hodgson’s daughter offered a tribute, recalling a kind, bearded man at the dinner table. Down-to-earth. Eternally relatable.

Close your eyes, breathe, and let that piano introduction wash over you. Then listen to the words again. Rick and Roger were trying to warn us. Millions sang along, yet few seemed to heed them.

I say it again, many speak. So, few really listen.

Hunter is a storyteller and like Shakespeare, his phrases can easily be pulled out of the context of their settings and used to give meaning to various things, depending on how they are needed at any given moment. Hunter may have borrowed some lyrics from the Bible, when he wrote, “I call it beggar’s tomb”, as Jesus tells a parable about a beggar a poor man that covered with sores and longing to eat what fell from the rich man’s table,and Jesus also had a friend named Lazarus who was raised from the dead and called out of his tomb.Hunter had varied reading habits, and he may have taken some lyrics from the‘Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam’(Persia, c. 1120) which says, “I came like Water, and like Wind I go.” Hunter wrote, “Like the morning sun you come and like the wind you go.”

1. Poor Poor Pitiful Me

> [Poor Poor Pitiful Me – A Candid Revelation from the Seedy Side of Life. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #WarrenZevon#LindaRonstadt](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/07/poor-poor-pitiful-me-a-candid-revelation-from-the-seedy-side-of-life-musicislife-tedtockscovers-warrenzevon-lindaronstadt/)

I opened this feature by suggesting that ‘Poor Poor Pitiful Me’ is Warren Zevon in a nutshell. It’s a self-mocking song that grins through misfortune while taunting death, and I argue that nobody turned pain and disaster into dark comedy quite like Zevon did. This is why Warren Zevon is songwriter #3 on my Mount Rushmore of lyricists. Top marks to any Ted Tocks Covers reader who can identify the man who rounds out this esteemed list.

This feature traces the wild road that culminated in his 1976 self-titled album. Zevon had already burned through a failed record deal and scraped by as a jingle writer and touring keyboardist. Alcoholism shadowed roughly half his life, and he cheerfully described himself as deeply anti-social. Jackson Browne produced the comeback record, and the song’s mix of suicide, domestic abuse and sadomasochism was hardly typical rock fare. Zevon refused to dissect his lyrics.

Linda Ronstadt made ‘Poor Poor Pitiful Me’ a hit, reaching #31 on the Billboard chart with her ‘Simple Dreams’ version. She approached the seedier verses warily, so she and Browne reworked one from a female point of view. She saw the song as the purest expression of male vanity. The hit validated Zevon and showcased a circle of admirers who stuck with him despite his unpredictable, often toxic behaviour.

My heart overflows in the closing. Zevon died in 2003, just weeks after ‘The Wind’ arrived, at only 56. More than twenty years on, his absence still stings. Few writers combine his melodic brilliance, his blood-drawing wit and his willingness to be honest about his own flaws. He made a remarkable final album after his terminal diagnosis, joked with David Letterman about outlasting Jim Morrison, and left the advice to enjoy every sandwich. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame recently honoured him (finally). As Dawes’ Taylor Goldsmith notes, Zevon showed that you can laugh at everything and still hold it sacred.

Yes…”Enjoy every sandwich.”

I was in the second row.

Me and my friend Steve spent the day at Ontario Place and the Canadian National Exhibition before rolling into the old CNE Stadium to see Neil Young and the International Harvesters. Neil had just released his ‘Old Ways’ album.

[Video 28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xzohbrqa4H8)

With Neil Young you never knew what was coming, but in my world, as an 18-year-old lost in the uncertainty between high school and university Neil was like my spiritual guide and if he told me the lesson for the day was going to take me back to his country roots then I was all ears. ‘Old Ways’ became my gateway to all that was good about authentic country music, not the formulaic crap that passes for country today.

Steve bought the album, the day it was released, just days before the show and within hours he dropped by my house with a cassette recording for my listening pleasure. When we arrived at the CNE by train, I spotted a guy wearing a Grateful Dead t-shirt that said:

> If you get confused listen to the music play.”

I knew I was in the right place. These words exist as my spiritual guide to this very day. Words to live by.

I pointed it out to Steve, and he just nodded and smiled. No words needed to be spoken.

Back in the ‘80s it was not uncommon to arrive at a concert and be surprised by the opening act. Information like this did not spread as rapidly as it does today through the internet. So, when Kris Kristofferson and his band, the Borderlords, walked out on the stage, I was blown away. I knew enough about him to know he was a living legend, but in retrospect, he was amid painting his own masterpiece. In many ways his set that day was both an homage to his past greatness and a dress rehearsal for the new heights to which he would ascend.

He played ‘Sunday Morning Coming Down’

> [Sunday Mornin’ Coming Down – Don’t Forget That Name. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #KrisKristofferson #JohnnyCash](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2025/09/28/sunday-mornin-coming-down-dont-forget-that-name-musicislife-tedtockscovers-kriskristofferson-johnnycash/)

And ‘Me and Bobby McGee’

> [Me and Bobby McGee – Freedom’s just another word. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #JanisJoplin #KrisKristofferson #RogerMiller](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2018/03/21/me-and-bobby-mcgee/)

As well as ‘Help Me Make It Through the Night’.

[Video 29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CksF7Kr7Drw)

But when he played ‘They Killed Him’ I felt something that I had never really experienced before. There was a message. Kris was delivering it like a prophet on the mount. He was not mincing words. It was intense. Blistering. Every word was delivered so emphatically that anyone in his presence that day must have felt the magnitude.

> There was a man named Mahatma Ghandi  
> He would not bow down, he would not fight  
> He knew the deal was down and dirty  
> And nothing wrong could make it right away  
>   
> But he knew his duty, and the price he had to pay  
> Just another holy man who tried to make a stand  
> MY GOD, THEY KILLED HIM!  
>   
> Another man from Atlanta, Georgia  
> By the name of Martin Luther King  
> He shook the land like rolling thunder  
> And made the bells of freedom ring today  
>   
> With a dream of beauty that they could not burn away  
> Just another holy man who dared to be a friend  
> MY GOD, THEY KILLED HIM!  
>   
> The only son of God Almighty  
> The holy one called Jesus Christ  
> Healed the lame and fed the hungry  
> And for his love they took his life away  
>   
> On the road to glory where the story never ends  
> Just the holy son of man we’ll never understand  
> MY GOD, THEY KILLED HIM!  
>   
> Sing about Mahatma Ghandi  
> Sing of Martin Luther King  
> Sing Of Jesus Christ Almighty  
> And the brothers Kennedy”

‘They Killed Him’ is a timeless warning about history repeating itself.

It’s the anguish that runs through ‘They Killed Him’ that sells the song. Kristofferson’s pen and his particularly unflinching way of looking at the world is a bonus. The man was a Rhodes Scholar and a Captain in the U.S. Army as a helicopter pilot. Kristofferson never wrote comfortable songs, and this one might be his least comfortable of all, because it doesn’t ask us to mourn three men, it asks us to indict ourselves.

Thoughtfully, the song moves through three figures who, on the surface, have almost nothing in common: Mahatma Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., and Jesus Christ. A Hindu independence leader, a Black Baptist preacher from the American South, and a Jewish carpenter from Roman-occupied Judea, separated by centuries and continents and creeds. Kristofferson managed to line them up deliberately, because what unites them is the point of the song. Each preached love as a weapon stronger than violence. Each asked people to turn away from hatred, from vengeance, from tribalism. And each was murdered for it. This did not happen despite the message. It happened because of it.

That’s the knockout punch that Kris Kristofferson delivered on that August day in 1985, and I still feel the pain. This isn’t a song about three isolated tragedies. It’s a song about a pattern. Kristofferson is essentially asking, how many times does humanity need to kill the person telling us to stop killing each other before we notice what we’re doing? The refrain isn’t just descriptive, it’s accusatory. It is pointed at all of us, not at some distant villain in history. We didn’t just fail to protect these men. We built the conditions that made their deaths almost inevitable, because a message of radical love threatens every system built on power, control, and fear.

As I type, monsters walk among us. They exist to destroy democracy and the free world. Three of the evillest people to ever exist.

Trump, Netanyahu and Putin and their equally evil cabal of sycophants.

It’s undeniable, yet about a third of the global population blindly follow these architects of destruction.

My God!

Back to the music, as legends go, the connection between Kris Kristofferson and Johnny Cash is borderline mythical.

Long before he was a Highwayman, Kris Kristofferson was a janitor. In the mid-1960s, he’d traded his impressing credentials for a job sweeping floors at Columbia Records’ Nashville studio. Here, he was close enough to the action to slip his own songs to anyone who would listen. He’d already tried the polite route with Johnny Cash. He offered demo tapes and brief exchanges between sessions, but this approach got him nowhere.

Ever resourceful, he switched tactics. Kristofferson had learned to fly helicopters in the Army, and as the story goes, he borrowed a chopper and flew it out to Cash’s place on Old Hickory Lake. He set it down on the lawn. Cash came out expecting trouble and found a shaggy ex-soldier with a tape in one hand and a beer in the other, depending on which version you believe. According to Kris Kristofferson, the Johnny Cash recollection was slightly embellished for dramatic effect.

> It was still kind of an invasion of privacy that I wouldn’t recommend. To be honest, I don’t think he was there… John had a pretty creative memory.”

The song on that tape was the aforementioned ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’. Cash recorded it in 1970. It won Country Music Awards Song of the Year. Kris Kristofferson went from janitor to one of the most covered songwriters in country music almost overnight.

Whether the beer was real, whether it was one landing or several increasingly desperate attempts, hardly matters. What matters is the image of a man landing an actual aircraft on your property because he believed in a song that much. Cash believed in it enough to build a career-redefining record around it, and enough to pull Kristofferson into the orbit that eventually became the Highwaymen.

This is a prelude to what years later became the first released recording of ‘They Killed Him’. He released it as a single in December of 1984. Both The Highwaymen and Kris Kristofferson’s ‘Repossessed’ (1986) were produced by legendary producer Chips Moman.

[Video 30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWZULirls6M)

By the time Farm Aid rolled around in 1986 Kristofferson’s status had been restored to its past form.

> Here’s one for the heroes”

Connections to his appearance at Farm Aid were all over the place. From Neil Young and Willie Nelson to Bob Dylan and beyond. Here is ‘They Killed Him’ from that July day in 1986.

[Video 31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LAejrW075Zo)

Some of the credit for the establishment of Farm Aid has gone to Bob Dylan who made a statement from the stage during his appearance at Live Aid in 1985.

> I hope that some of the money that’s raised for the people in Africa—maybe they could just take a little bit of it, maybe one or two million, maybe—and use it, say, to pay the mortgages on some of the farms that the farmers here owe to the banks.”

Pretty Boy Floyd would have smiled down on Bob Dylan when he uttered those words. In July of 1986, just one week after Kris Kristofferson performed at Farm Aid, Dylan released the album ‘Knocked Out Loaded’ and track two was ‘They Killed Him’. This is an epic performance that features the legendary Al Kooper on keyboards and some backing vocals that stir ones’ emotions, especially when the children’s chorus kicks in.

[Video 32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XokAdcVvUCQ)

At around the same time Bob Dylan was working with the Grateful Dead on the divisive ‘Dylan and the Dead’ collaboration. This recording emerged from the San Raphael, California sessions. Just one more example of how far Kris Kristofferson’s words extended.

[Video 33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LUCjAuMSydY)

No discussion of ‘They Killed Him’ would be complete without sharing this live recording by The Highwaymen. This is from their famous 1990 Nassau County Coliseum concert. Seeing Willie, Waylon, Johnny and Kris together and delivering this message is something special. It just serves to remind me that when I saw Kristofferson five years earlier all of this was brewing in the background.

[Video 34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9HGk87kheug)

For the final cover version, I discovered this beautiful offering from Kate Campbell and yet another Nashville legend, Spooner Oldham (see ‘[Cry Like a Baby](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2021/06/14/cry-like-a-baby-a-salute-to-a-legendary-side-man-musicislife-tedtockscovers-spooneroldham-danpenn-theboxtops-percysledge-wilsonpickett-arethafranklin-ettajames-cher-janisjoplin-lindaron/)’). This is from Campbell’s album ‘For the Living of These Days’. The only thing better than Kat’s delivery is Spooner Oldham’s piano accompaniment. Beautiful.

[Video 35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aSvhcnY7RMU)

On this day that we pay tribute to Kris Kristofferson, two years from the day he left us, what makes this a Ted Tocks Covers kind of song is how uncomfortably current it remains. Kristofferson wrote it decades ago, but the mechanism he’s describing still haunts us. We still watch reformers, whistleblowers, and peacemakers get vilified, marginalized, or worse, while the systems they challenge absorb the shock and carry on largely unchanged. It’s astonishing to see freedom of the press in jeopardy while an addle minded madman runs roughshod over the rule of law. Meanwhile we erect monuments to people after they’re gone that we refused to build space for while they were alive. That’s the “reaping what we’ve sown” undercurrent running beneath the song. It is plain to see that division, retaliation, and complicity don’t just disappear when the news cycle moves on. They compound. They come back around, dressed in different clothes and a goofy red hat, wearing a different decade’s headlines, and we act surprised every time.

Kristofferson’s genius here is refusing to let the song become a history lesson you can file as something from the past. He’s naming a cycle, and cycles don’t stay in the past. They recur until the pattern is broken. The song doesn’t offer resolution or comfort. There’s no bridge where hope swoops in to save the day. For Kristofferson that was intentional. He trusted his audience enough to leave them with the discomfort, because comfort is exactly what lets these patterns repeat unchallenged.

Listening to ‘They Killed Him’ today, in a moment still thick with division, scapegoating, and short memories, feels less like revisiting an old protest song and more like looking in the mirror.

Kristofferson wasn’t writing an epitaph. He was writing a warning label. One we apparently still need.

Once again, I say it.

MY GOD!

How can we be so obtuse?

# [Nevermind – 35 Years Later We Still Find Ourselves Saying Oh Well Whatever. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers#Nirvana](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/24/nevermind-35-years-later-we-still-find-ourselves-saying-oh-well-whatever-musicislife-tedtockscovers-nirvana/)

[September 24, 2026 September 24, 2026](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/24/nevermind-35-years-later-we-still-find-ourselves-saying-oh-well-whatever-musicislife-tedtockscovers-nirvana/) ~ [tedlindsay0170](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/author/tedlindsay0170/) ~ [1 Comment](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/24/nevermind-35-years-later-we-still-find-ourselves-saying-oh-well-whatever-musicislife-tedtockscovers-nirvana/#comments)

[Video 38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TDeBi34OtE)

Thirty-five years ago, on September 24, 1991, a rough around the edges band from Seattle released an album that would completely rewrite the rules of popular music. Nirvana’s ‘Nevermind’ didn’t just top charts, it toppled an entire era of glossy, hair-metal excess and replaced it with something rawer, angrier, and quite frankly, far more honest.

At the time, nobody expected much. ‘Nevermind’ was Nirvana’s major label debut and only their second full-length record, recorded that spring at Sound City Studios in Van Nuys, California, with producer Butch Vig at the helm. The band walked into those sessions as underground favorites with a devoted but modest following. Nobody, including the band members themselves, predicted they were about to blow up the music industry.

The album started slow. By no means race up the charts overnight. But then something happened. MTV started playing the video for ‘Smells Like Teen Spirit’.

> [Smells Like Teen Spirit – An accidental hit and a Gen X anthem. Stupid and contagious but it works. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #Nirvana #WeirdAlYankovic #PaulAnka](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2018/11/28/smells-like-teen-spirit/)

Radio stations couldn’t stop spinning it, and word of mouth did the rest. By January 1992, Nevermind had done the unthinkable. It knocked Michael Jackson’s ‘Dangerous’ out of the #1 spot on the Billboard 200. Here is Dave Grohl briefly summarizing Nirvana’s unlikely ascent.

> Michael Jackson was huge. Whitney Houston was huge. Michael Bolton was huge. There was no place for us in that.”

A band that had been playing dive bars a couple years earlier was suddenly the biggest thing in music.

What made ‘Nevermind’ so powerful wasn’t just ‘Teen Spirit’, though that song alone became a generational anthem, practically overnight shorthand for disaffected youth everywhere. It was the sheer depth of the record.

‘Come as You Are’ showed off Nirvana’s knack for melody wrapped in murky, unsettling guitar tones.

> [Come As You Are – A significant date in relation to the ‘Seattle’ music scene. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #KurtCobain #Nirvana #AliceInChains #LayneStaley #KillingJoke #TheDamned #DaveGrohl #MadSeason #MikeMcCready #StoneGossard #ShawnSmith #Brad #LeoMoracchioli#LittleRoy](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2020/04/05/come-as-you-are-a-significant-date-in-relation-to-the-seattle-music-scene-musicislife-tedtockscovers-kurtcobain-nirvana-aliceinchains-laynestaley-killingjoke-thedamned-davegrohl-madse/)

‘Lithium’ swung between quiet vulnerability and explosive catharsis in a way that felt genuinely new.

‘In Bloom’ took aim at the very mainstream audience the band was about to inherit, dripping with irony that most listeners probably missed.

> [In Bloom – You gotta love these pretty songs. If you don’t get it…#Nevermind. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #Nirvana #SturgillSimpson](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2018/09/28/in-bloom/)

Track after track, Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, and Dave Grohl proved this wasn’t a one-hit fluke. This was a band that had something real to say.

The ripple effects are almost impossible to overstate. ‘Nevermind’ didn’t just sell records, it killed off the party-rock dominance of the late ’80s almost single-handedly. Suddenly labels were scrambling to sign anything resembling “alternative”, and bands from Pearl Jam to Soundgarden to countless others found doors thrown open that had been locked for years. Grunge went from a regional Pacific Northwest scene to a global movement in a matter of months, and much of that shift traces directly back to this one record.

Thirty-five years later, ‘Nevermind’ still hits with the same urgency. Its production, once considered a little too polished by purists, now sounds perfectly balanced, loud enough to rock but clear enough to let every riff and lyric land. New generations keep discovering it, keep finding themselves in its mix of frustration, melody, and raw emotion.

That’s the real legacy of ‘Nevermind’. It wasn’t just an album that sold millions of copies. It was a cultural reset button, one that continues to influence how rock music sounds and feels more than three decades on.

Admittedly, time got the better of me this week and my goal of featuring a track-by-track post fell by the wayside. Instead, enjoy this feature by Stephn Hill of Metal Hammer. This is a great article because he digs deep.

[https://www.loudersound.com/features/we-put-together-the-ultimate-nevermind-covers-album](https://www.loudersound.com/features/we-put-together-the-ultimate-nevermind-covers-album)

Maybe that’s the real secret behind ‘Nevermind’ and its staying power: it never talks down to anyone. Kurt Cobain had an uncanny ability to capture contradiction, the way someone can feel fiercely self-reliant and totally lost in the same breath.

It’s all in the liner notes.

> Spring is here again, tender age in bloom, he knows not what it means, sell the kids for food, we can have some more • The water is so yellow, I’m a healthy student, you’re my vitamins • Take your time, hurry up, the choice is yours, don’t be late • And just maybe I’m to blame for all I’ve heard but I’m not sure, I’m so excited I can’t wait to meet you there but I don’t care • I don’t care if it’s old, I don’t mind if I don’t have a mind, get away from your home • Have to have poison skin, give an inch take a smile • Never met a wise man, if so it’s a woman, gotta find a way to find a way, I had better wait • One more special message to go, as defense I’m neutered and spayed, what the hell am I trying to say? I got so high that I scratched till I bled • The second coming came in last and out of the closet • At the end of the rainbow and your rope • Don’t hurt yourself, I want some help to help myself, she’s just as bored as me • I’ve got this friend you see, who makes me feel, I don’t regret a thing • And the animals I’ve trapped have all become my pets • Our little group has always been and always will until the end, with the lights out it’s less dangerous, here we are now, entertain us, I feel stupid and contagious, here we are now entertain us, a mulatto, an albino, a mosquito, my libido, yay, yay, a denial, I’m worse at what I do best and for this gift I feel blessed, I found it hard, it was hard to find, oh well, whatever, nevermind”

A universal rite of passage for many is to be torn between defiance and doubt. We often feel unsure what to do with feelings that don’t resolve neatly. Truth be told that is not a teenage problem or a ’90s problem. That’s a human problem, and it’s exactly why 15-year-olds discovering this record today feel just as seen as the 15-year-olds who first heard it in 1991.

That’s the thing about true angst. It doesn’t fade with the decade. Everyone stumbles through the same messy plain of confusion, alienation, longing to belong while also wanting to be left alone. Nirvana didn’t try to solve any these issues. They just sat with it, turned it up loud, and let it feel less lonely.

Thirty-five years on, ‘Nevermind’ isn’t a museum piece. It’s still blasting out of car speakers, still soundtracking bad days and cathartic ones, still hanging out with anyone who needs it.

What does timeless really mean?

It is not that something stays the same. It keeps finding new people who need exactly what it has to offer.

# [Uncle John’s Band – Ain’t No Time to Hate. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #GratefulDead#RobertHunter](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/23/uncle-johns-band-aint-no-time-to-hate-musicislife-tedtockscovers-gratefuldead-roberthunter/)

[September 23, 2026 September 22, 2026](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/23/uncle-johns-band-aint-no-time-to-hate-musicislife-tedtockscovers-gratefuldead-roberthunter/) ~ [tedlindsay0170](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/author/tedlindsay0170/) ~ [5 Comments](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2026/09/23/uncle-johns-band-aint-no-time-to-hate-musicislife-tedtockscovers-gratefuldead-roberthunter/#comments)

[Video 39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D2zItg1sBJg)

Before the first chord lands, all Ted Tocks wants to tell you by way of an introduction is that to me ‘Uncle John’s Band’ is a treasure trove of Americana. It is intriguing to note that during a moment in time when whatever America once was seems so far in the rear-view mirror that a glance back at this Grateful Dead classic might do us some good.

As a song ‘Uncle John’s Band’ has always felt like sitting on a front porch with the screen door swinging. It is presented in the folk tradition with a hint of the Appalachian twang that was no doubt intended. From there we can almost feel the gospel choir and the barroom singalong, all while wandering through the same open field. Jerry Garcia and Robert Hunter wrote ‘Uncle John’s Band’ in the latter half of 1969. Although the post Woodstock era seems far removed, it still has the feel of something that is always with us, waiting for somebody to pick it up and hum it back into our collective conscience.

Through Ted Tocks Covers I have spent a lot of years thinking about what makes human connection last, and I keep coming back to the same place. When I meet people, there is one thing I want to know.

> Are you kind?”

In many ways that is where we all begin. Everything flows from there.

Not necessarily “Where are you from?” or “What do you do?” Not even “What do you believe?”

That information tends to flow within the course of the conversation.

Kindness is the doorway. If you’re kind, we can talk about the rest. We can disagree over coffee and still leave as friends. We can trade stories and harmonies and hard-earned mistakes.

That’s what the Grateful Dead understood as a band. The harmonies here are a conversation among people who are listening to each other. Nobody is shouting over anybody. The invitation is right there in the line.

> Come hear Uncle John’s Band, playing to the tide”

So, settle in. Let the tempo breathe. There’s room on this porch for everyone who shows up with an open heart and a little curiosity.

Here is Ted Tocks Covers take on ‘Uncle John’s Band’.

In the annals of the Grateful Dead catalogue ‘Uncle John’s Band’ began to appear as part of the band’s setlists in late 1969.

Dick’s Picks offers this instrumental version from a November 8 show at Fillmore Auditorium in San Francisco.

[Video 40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VQ5RSzuOcUQ)

According to Grateful Dead setlists, the first time the band played it in its entirety was December 4, 1969, just two days before the ill-fated Altamont concert.

[Video 41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bfq2UloMjPY)

For the Grateful Dead the transition to the style presented in ‘Uncle John’s Band’ represented a seismic shift. It was recorded as a track for ‘Workingman’s Dead’ and released in June of 1970.

The album title was an ode to Merle Haggard and his song ‘Workin’ Man Blues’. Gone were the sprawling psychedelic jams. Instead, the group moved to a more roots-oriented sound steeped in folk, country, and Americana traditions. The influence of artists like Haggard can be heard throughout the record, which traded cosmic exploration for songs about ordinary people, hard work, and everyday struggles.

[Video 42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6EwK0NsKdDY)

Here is Bob Weir speaking to this very point.

> We were listening to the radio at the time and there was a tune Merle Haggard did called ‘Workin’ Man Blues’. Jerry and I in particular, and most of the guys were real fond of that tune. It incorporated an aesthetic that we appreciated.”

In keeping with the period, ‘Uncle John’s Band’ was featured as the A-side of a single that was backed by Robert Hunter’s summation of the Altamont fiasco and the dark demise of the Woodstock generation, ‘New Speedway Boogie’.

> [New Speedway Boogie – Things went down we don’t understand but I think in time we will. #MusicisLife #TedTocksCovers #GratefulDead #RobertHunter #WidespreadPanic #BeauSassersEscapePlan #CourtneyBarnett #DogsinaPile](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2021/06/23/new-speedway-boogie-things-went-down-we-dont-understand-but-i-think-in-time-we-will-musicislife-tedtockscovers-gratefuldead-roberthunter-widespreadpanic-beausassersescapeplan-courtn/)

Much of the intrinsic value of the lyrical content during this era of the Dead stems from the fact that Robert Hunter began touring with the band; taking stock of the scene. Frequently, the songs developed in real time. Here is Phil Lesh’s recollection of the ‘Workingman’s Dead’ track list from his 2005 autobiography ‘Searching for the Sound’.

> The song lyrics reflected an ‘old, weird’ America that perhaps never was … The almost miraculous appearance of these new songs would also generate a massive paradigm shift in our group mind: from the mind-munching frenzy of a seven-headed fire-breathing dragon to the warmth and serenity of a choir of chanting cherubim. Even the album cover reflects this new direction: The cover for‘Aoxomoxoa’is colorful and psychedelic, and that of‘Workingman’s Dead’ is monochromatic and sepia.”

Additional enhancement was brought forth through the harmonies which were famously attributed to the band’s friendship with Crosby Stills and Nash. Here is Mickey Hart discussing the benefits of paying attention to this trio’s vocal stylings and how it reinforced the value of the lyrical content.

> Stills lived with me for three months around the time of CSN’s first record, and he and David Crosby really turned Jerry and Bobby onto the voice as the holy instrument. You know, ‘Hey, is this what a voice can do?’ That turned us away from pure improvisation and more toward songs.”

Jerry Garcia was equally enthusiastic.

> Hearing those guys sing and how nice they sounded together, we thought, ‘We can try that. Let’s work on it a little’.”

As always, the Grateful Dead’s ace in the hole was having a lyricist like Robert Hunter who could capture the spirit and soul of any given moment in a unique way. Dissecting the lyrics of ‘Uncle John’s Band’ is a lot like walking through U.S. history with the ghosts of its sordid past.

Hunter starts with a warning combined with some delicate words of advice, that the first days are the hardest. Then he undercuts the comfort with the “Easy Street” line, which is a Depression-era phrase for security. His point is that comfort is where the danger hides, which to his credit is what Dickens spent whole novels saying.

He wants to use the song as a vehicle to take us through life, but before a decision is made Robert Hunter asks the question that drives the song:

> Are you kind?”

It’s a strange thing to ask in a rock song. It’s less a test of belief than of character. It becomes the promise.

To begin the next verse Hunter refers to “Buck dancer’s choice” which is an old Appalachian fiddle-tune name, and the phrase implies the dancer picks the tune. So, the advice is to take the offered wisdom. The phrase may have been drawn from the poem ‘Buckdancer’s Choice’ by James Dickey.

> It is called Buckdancer’s Choice.
> 
> 
> For years, they have all been dying
> 
> 
> Out, the classic buck-and-wing men”

Metaphorically speaking with respect to ‘Uncle John’s Band’ we arrive at a moment where one faces limited or final options yet retains the personal freedom to choose how to act or express themselves”

For pop culture purposes, James Dickey also wrote the novel which inspired the film, ‘Deliverance’.

In that same verse Hunter opts to close the passage with the words “the fire from the ice” which is a nod to the Robert Frost poem ‘Fire and Ice’. Everyone knows the rules, but only experience teaches you to tell the two apart. Here is the passage.

> Some say the world will end in fire,
> 
> 
> Some say in ice.
> 
> 
> From what I’ve tasted of desire
> 
> 
> I hold with those who favor fire.
> 
> 
> But if it had to perish twice,
> 
> 
> I think I know enough of hate
> 
> 
> To say that for destruction ice
> 
> 
> Is also great
> 
> 
> And would suffice.”

This contemplation leads to the invitation.

> Will you come with me?  
> Won’t you come with me?  
> Whoa, oh, what I want to know  
> Will you come with me?”

The verse about the cannonball walls and “don’t tread on me” jumps to Revolutionary-era America and the Gadsden flag. Hunter wrote these words in 1969, a year of dissent, so the mock-Southern “Goddamn, I declare” reads as a wry look at a country fortified against its own neighbours. Read this again and remind yourself that you are reading it in 2026.

‘DONT TREAD ON ME’ is a well-known political slogan going back to the American Revolution. Combine this with a visual reference to the Gadsden Flag which shows a timber rattlesnake ready to strike and things get even more ominous. It’s no surprise that this slogan was also key to the ‘Tea Party’ movement which moved America further to the political right.

According to Robert Hunter, the words to this refrain were carefully chosen. He had “god damn, Uncle John’s mad” running through his mind, but the declaration turned into, “Come hear Uncle John’s Band.” It softened what was a buildup to conflict into something more galvanizing. In Hunter’s words, the moment of creative revelation was the kind where;

> …Sparkles start coming out of your eyes.”

The chorus is the invitation. Uncle John’s band plays “to the tide,” and the tide won’t wait. The line “Come with me or go alone” is the Dead’s whole approach to their audience. They offered a road, not a doctrine.

As the new verse unfolds a new image is presented in the form of a crow.

Applying my hasty research to traditional southern and Appalachian-style humor, the crow is depicted as passing down absurd, nonsensical tall tales or unchanging truths about life’s silly routines. Here, the crow verse feels like Aesop’s Fables crossed with Edgar Allan Poe. A crow that knows only one story, about coming like the morning sun and leaving like the wind, echoes Ecclesiastes and the eternal truth that everything passes.

A deeper dive led me to this song by Johnny Horton, whose work in relating history through songs written by Jimmy Driftwood helped generations understand America’s past.

> It’s the same old tale that the crow told me  
> Way down yonder by the sycamore tree”

The music does as much as the words. The tune keeps shifting between waltz-like and straight time, which suits a song about time slipping away. The harmonies which existed as a new experiment for this band feel communal, like a chorus of neighbours.

[Video 62](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ugTEBmGdrMw)

What makes ‘Uncle John’s Band’ endure isn’t just the melody or the harmonies, it’s what happened every single time the Dead played it live. The song didn’t just entertain a crowd; it assembled one. Deadheads weren’t spectators watching a band perform a tune about a riverside gathering, they always were the gathering, night after night, venue after venue. On a spiritual level, the occasional imperfections were part of the magic. When Jerry mixed up a lyric in a song that half-jokingly included the lyric “how does the song go?” nobody groaned. They grinned right along with him, because it was proof the moment was alive, unscripted, happening in real time.

Then the band would peel away from the campfire warmth and dive into that startling trademark jam with odd meters and modal turns, like the song itself was daring you to follow it somewhere stranger. Just like a meandering river. Here is where we get a microcosm of the Grateful Dead scene. Comfort intertwined with risk. Light filters its way through a shadow. One could barely find their footing in the weirdness before the band snapped back to that chorus, and suddenly it was a singalong again with thousands of hands clapping the beat. In this moment the crowd became the rhythm section or the pulse. It’s hard to think of another song that could swing between danger and delight and back with that much grace and still leave you dancing the whole way through.

There is something about Robert Hunter’s lyrics that increases their significance the longer you sit with them. Imagine a crow narrating the arc of a life, appearing and vanishing like mortality itself. Such a perfect closing image as we fortify ourselves with walls built of cannonballs. Is it a sacred monument or a societal indictment?

Robert Hunter never tells us which, and that’s the point. ‘Uncle John’s Band’ holds all of it at once. It is joy and unease. It is both an invitation and a warning. It is folk simplicity and a disturbing strangeness. He lays it all out through the Grateful Dead sound without ever resolving the tension.

Hunter himself warned us of this many years ago as he teased the inspiration.

> I was thinking about the — sort of the hippie, self-congratulatory thing that we’d really conquered all this. You know, here, we’ve got — we’ve ended the Vietnam War. We’ve done this, the other thing. And then, you know, things looking rosy. No, no, it’s — liberty, the price is eternal vigilance.”

Maybe that’s why, all these years later, it still functions as an invitation. Come hear the band. Sit by the river. Just don’t expect the ground to stay steady beneath you.

Eternal vigilance disappeared and in our complacency we handed the wheel of the bus over to somebody new.

Now we are desperately lost.

It was 50 years ago today that Wild Cherry hit #1 with ‘Play that Funky Music’.

In the period that led up to this success Wild Cherry was facing some serious concerns about their future. As a band Wild Cherry would have been categorized as hard rock. In the ‘rust belt’ area they had a reputation as a quality cover band that also shared some catchy original material. During the latter half of 1975 and early 1976 they were feeling the shift in the live music scene. Audiences were gravitating to the disco and as a result club owners were hiring acts that played music that had a dance appeal. Here is lead singer Rob Parissi’s summation during a 2017 interview with Harry Connick Jr.

> We were a rock band, and disco music was coming in. Rock clubs were closing down, and discos were opening up. And we were a hard-working band playing four, five, six nights a week.”

Wild Cherry was in an awkward position, and it led to some internal strife within the band. Parissi pleaded with his mates to modify their presentation but the other four were adamant.

No disco.

So Parissi did the next best thing. He imagined a disco song that incorporated elements of hard rock, funk, Motown and soul influences. Sounds of the Ohio Players, meshed with ‘[Superstition](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2018/10/28/superstition/)’ by Stevie Wonder and Jeff Beck’ and ‘[How Many More Times](https://tedtockscovers.wordpress.com/2025/03/09/how-many-more-times-a-blues-improv-with-led-zeppelin-musicislife-tedtockscovers-ledzeppelin-howlinwolf-albertking/)’ by Led Zeppelin were swirling in Parissi’s head.

> I finally told the guys ‘how about if Led Zeppelin did ‘That’s The Way I Like It’ (KC & The Sunshine Band)? So, I walked out and I wrote down exactly what was going on with us. I had the first two verses and chorus written by the time we hit the stage. And I wrote the last verse in the car on the way home.”

Guitarist, Bryan Bassett elaborated on this story in an interview with Joe Grushecky that harkened back on the Pittsburgh music scene, specifically a downtown bar called 2001 with a primarily Black audience.

> ‘Play That Funky Music’ is pretty autobiographical and quite literal. Club work was getting scarce if you didn’t play dance music, so we decided to change. Someone actually did say that to us- play that funky music white boy- insinuating that if we didn’t, we probably wouldn’t be working much longer. I remember it happening at the 2001 Club in downtown Pittsburgh, which had turned into a big disco. We were still playing Kiss, Led Zeppelin and Foghat. Someone came up to our drummer Ron and said, you better play that funky music white boy. He told that to Rob in the dressing room and I believe Rob started writing that song right then.”

[Video 64](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hHXcnO3SB-c)

Sheldon Cooper doesn’t do casual listening. Put “Play That Funky Music” on in a car with him and Leonard, and what should be three minutes of dance-floor joy turns into a seminar. That’s the joke embedded in ‘Big Bang Theory’ and the Season 8 episode ‘The Skywalker Incursion’. A simple road-trip needle-drop becomes Sheldon dissecting the song’s internal logic instead of just enjoying it.

And as I attempting to share in this feature, there is something to dissect. Wild Cherry’s 1976 smash is built on an obvious contradiction. A hard rock guitarist recounts how he used to turn his nose up at funk or more aptly stated, disco, only for the song itself to become one of the funkiest records ever pressed to vinyl. The narrator disavows the genre in the very act of mastering it. That’s the kind of quandary that would catch in Sheldon’s brain. It is a statement that undoes itself the moment it’s spoken, not unlike Bertrand Russell’s famous set-theory headache. Does the set of all sets that don’t contain themselves contain itself?

My head is beginning to spin but…

…Ask the question sincerely and the answer collapses in on itself either way. Sheldon, being Sheldon, apparently couldn’t resist reaching for that comparison and as a result he drags a three-minute funk/rock standard into the company of one of the twentieth century’s great, logical paradoxes, because to him, everything is fair game for discussion, including a song about a guy who apparently didn’t know what he was afraid of.

What I love about the scene, all specifics aside, is what it says about how great music works. ‘Play That Funky Music’ survives because it doesn’t need to make logical sense. Some music genres rarely do, and quite frankly it’s better for it. Rhythm forgives paradox. Initially, in an uncharacteristically disarming moment Sheldon who demands the lyrics hold up to formal scrutiny; before throwing his hands up to say;

> Music should just be fun.”

Meanwhile, the rest of us have been dancing, through the years, reference and all.

Like so many cross-genre songs of high profile and intriguing influence, there are several cover versions of ‘Play That Funky Music’. For today’s feature Ted Tocks has reduced it to a six pack of tributes from as wide a range of acts as I could gather.

Roxanne was formed in Riverside, California in 1986 by frontman Jamie Brown and bassist Joe Infante. They quickly rose through the ranks of the Los Angeles hard rock scene alongside the hair metal movement, eventually landing a record deal and releasing their self-titled debut album in 1986. That album included a cover of ‘Play That Funky Music’. The one I have chosen is a slightly rawer promotional release.

[Video 65](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vmgVmWCUJrQ)

Next up is Vanilla Ice who released ‘Play That Funky Music’ as a single along with ’Ice Ice Baby’ in 1989. Based on the strength of the single, independent record label, Ichiban signed Vanilla Ice to a record deal and the two songs were released on the LP, ‘Hooked’. Success soon followed, but so too did trouble. Naturally, Rob Parissi heard the Vanilla Ice version which for some bizarre reason Vanilla Ice did not credit Parissi. A lawsuit ensued and the copyright settlement awarded Rob Parissi with $500,000. In the end it was ‘Ice Ice Baby’ which generated the most interest, which began when a DJ accidentally flipped the record and played the B-side. That mistake helped Vanilla Ice pay for the lawsuit ruling.

[Video 66](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mruC7WRKPdI)

Paul Di’Anno is perhaps best known as the vocalist for Iron Maiden on their 1980 self-titled debut album, and their follow up ‘Killers’ in 1981. Sadly, Di’Anno crashed and burned, and Iron Maiden opted to fire Di’Anno following the ‘Killers’ tour. In 1997, Paul Di’Anno released ‘The World’s First Iron Man’ which drew moderate reviews from fans but for the purposes of this feature it included ‘Play That Funky Music’.

[Video 67](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U0ZpJ4GW0aM)

The award for most unusual cover goes to Leningrad Cowboys and the version that they offered on their 2006 album ‘Zombie Paradise’.

[Video 68](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HcELLOBWRR4)

In 2011, Prince embarked on his ‘Welcome 2’ tour which included 12 shows at The Forum in Los Angeles. The shows included five encores and when he came out for encore four he blew the audience away with ‘Play That Funky Music’. This is three minutes of Prince greatness.

[Video 69](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fDOcnuO5c04)

Every time Leo Moracchioli comes up in my search it is an automatic share because he always delivers high-quality performances. Enjoy this frenetic five minutes of ‘Play That Funky Music’ which is only enhanced by the boundless energy of his dancers. Remember what Sheldon said? Leo and his dancers personify this statement.

[Video 70](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m2fk0CY7LSM)

To quote Peter Griffin of ‘Family Guy’, do you want to know what really grinds my gears?

It is when people write off a song or an artist as a one hit wonder?

When this occurs, the work of an act is being marginalized. No consideration is given to the blood, sweat and tears that got them to the point that they could write, record, release and perform that hit. The journey to get to that point is a remarkable achievement. The success was the reward, and it should never be written off as a fluke. To some extent Wild Cherry is categorized in this space, even though the significance of this song is far reaching.

There is a lesson contained within the lyrics.

> Oh, but now it’s so much better (it’s so much better)  
> I’m funking out in every way  
> But I’ll never lose that feelin’ (you know, I won’t)  
> Of how I learned my lesson that day

When Rob Parissi and Wild Cherry opened their mind to a new sound what they created was a cross-cultural smash.

Borrowing from Sly and the Family Stone they shouted out that as an act they would take us higher.

And they did.

On this day in 1979, a fifteen-minute single with no chorus, no traditional hook, and three guys nobody had ever heard of trading boastful verses over a looped bassline started its climb up the charts. By January of 1980, ‘Rapper’s Delight’ by the Sugarhill Gang had cracked the top 40 of the Billboard Hot 100. In the big picture, the significance didn’t really register at the time, but it was the first rap song to do so. The music industry, largely dismissive of this new sound bubbling out of the NY/NJ area, treated it as a novelty. A fad. Something that would burn off by summer. Over forty-six years later, we know how that story continues to be told.

But to understand why ‘Rapper’s Delight’ worked, and why it endures, you have to look at three things: the record that quietly beat it to the punch, the song underneath its groove, and the woman who had the industry savvy to put the whole thing together.

Here is something you need to know. Before Sugarhill, there was a funk/disco band called Fatback

Truthfully, rap did not arrive in 1979. It had been flowing in parks, block parties, and community centers throughout New York for at least half a decade before anyone thought to put it on vinyl. The first commercially released rap record belongs to the Fatback Band, whose ‘King Tim III (Personality Jock)’ landed as a B-side to one of their more customary singles earlier in 1979.

It’s a great record, and historically it matters enormously. But it was buried on the flip side of a dance single, treated as a curiosity rather than a statement. It didn’t chart. It didn’t announce a movement. It planted a flag nobody noticed.

‘Rapper’s Delight’ approached it in a different way. It wasn’t hidden. It was the whole show. ‘Rapper’s Delight’ was dropped like an audacious front-and-center rhythm that rhymed over a beat so it could be the main event, not the bonus track. Famously, the groove that flowed underneath was ‘Good Times’ by Chic, which in and of itself was inspired by Kool and the Gang’s ‘Hollywood Swinging’.

[Video 73](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YK-cvcw3ngM)

Soon after, Queen borrowed that same foundation for ‘Another One Bites the Dust’, which was proof that the bassline had a gravitational pull strong enough to entice entire genres its way.
